conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: Is genital candidiasis a sexually transmitted infection?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: No — it is NOT an STI. It is the itchy, normal-pH, non-STI member of the vaginal-discharge trio (the key contrast with BV and trichomonas).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: Why does candida only sometimes cause infection despite colonising the vagina?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Candida can colonise the vagina asymptomatically and only causes infection when the local balance shifts — which is why the risk factors are all states that disturb the normal flora or immunity.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: What is the cleanest single discriminator between candida and BV/trichomonas?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Vaginal pH: candida has a NORMAL pH <4.5, whereas both BV and trichomonas have pH >4.5.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: Compare candida, BV and trichomonas by cause, discharge, odour, pH and partner treatment.
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Candida: yeast (not STI), thick white 'cottage cheese' discharge, non-offensive odour, pH <4.5, prominent itch, no partner Rx. BV: anaerobes (not STI), thin white/grey, fishy, pH >4.5, minimal itch, no partner Rx. Trichomonas: protozoan (STI), frothy yellow-green, offensive, pH >4.5, itchy, partner Rx needed.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: List the main risk factors for vaginal candidiasis.
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Diabetes mellitus (especially poorly controlled), broad-spectrum antibiotics (wipe out protective bacteria), pregnancy (high oestrogen), immunosuppression (steroids, HIV, chemotherapy), and other high-oestrogen states (sometimes the COCP).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: Why do broad-spectrum antibiotics predispose to thrush?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: They wipe out the protective vaginal bacteria (lactobacilli), disturbing the flora and allowing candida overgrowth.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: What is the classic discharge and dominant symptom of vaginal candidiasis?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: A thick, white, 'cottage cheese', non-offensive discharge, with vulval itch and irritation as the dominant symptom.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: What features of vulvitis may accompany candidiasis?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Superficial dyspareunia and external dysuria (from the inflamed vulva), with vulval erythema, fissuring, and satellite lesions on examination.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: Is a high vaginal swab routinely needed to diagnose candidiasis?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: No — if the picture is typical, diagnose clinically and treat. A swab (HVS for microscopy/culture) is reserved for recurrent, atypical, or treatment-failure cases.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: What is the key bedside test in the discharge differential, and candida's result?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Vaginal pH: candida gives a NORMAL pH <4.5 (vs BV/trichomonas pH >4.5).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: When is an HVS for microscopy/culture useful in candidiasis, and what can it identify?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: In recurrent, atypical, or treatment-failure cases — it can identify non-albicans species (e.g. Candida glabrata) which may be azole-resistant.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: Can candida be found on a cervical smear, and is a smear the diagnostic test?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Candida (hyphae/spores) may be an incidental Pap smear finding, but a smear is NOT the diagnostic test for thrush.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: What is the first-line treatment for uncomplicated candidiasis in a non-pregnant woman?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: A single-dose oral fluconazole 150 mg.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: What is the second-line treatment if oral therapy is contraindicated or not tolerated?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Clotrimazole 500 mg intravaginal pessary (single dose).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: What should be added if there are vulval symptoms?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: A topical imidazole cream (e.g. clotrimazole) applied to the vulva, alongside the oral or intravaginal treatment.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: How is candidiasis treated in pregnancy, and what must be avoided?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Do NOT use oral fluconazole (risk of congenital abnormalities). Use topical treatment only — an intravaginal azole (clotrimazole) pessary/cream, often a longer course (up to 7 days).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: How many symptomatic episodes per year define recurrent vaginal candidiasis?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: ≥4 symptomatic episodes per year.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: What is the workup for recurrent vaginal candidiasis?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Check compliance with previous treatment; confirm the diagnosis with HVS for MCS (species/resistance); check blood glucose/HbA1c to exclude diabetes; and exclude differentials such as lichen sclerosus, dermatitis and other causes of vulval itch.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: What is the induction–maintenance regimen for recurrent candidiasis?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Induction: oral fluconazole every 3 days for 3 doses (days 1, 4, 7). Maintenance: oral fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: Do partners of a woman with candidiasis need treatment?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: No — candidiasis is not sexually transmitted, so partners are not treated.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.front: What practical advice should be given about irritants and condoms in candidiasis?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Candidiasis (.back: Avoid vaginal irritants (soaps, douching); and note that some topical azoles can damage latex condoms and diaphragms.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: Why does BV matter in a sexual health (GUM) setting specifically?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: It is the single commonest cause of abnormal vaginal discharge presenting to GUM. The clinician's first job is to place it on the STI-vs-not-STI map: BV is NOT an STI but is sexually associated, and crucially it increases susceptibility to acquiring true STIs including HIV — so it is both a discharge to treat and a flag prompting full STI screening.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: Is bacterial vaginosis a sexually transmitted infection?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: No — it is NOT an STI, but it IS sexually associated (more common with new/multiple partners and unprotected sex). It can also occur in women who have never been sexually active, hence 'associated' not 'transmitted'.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: What is the underlying mechanism of BV?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: Loss of protective lactobacilli → vaginal pH rises above 4.5 → overgrowth of anaerobes, chiefly Gardnerella vaginalis. Everything flows from the loss of acidity.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: In GUM, why is getting the 'STI or not' call right so important for BV?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: Because it dictates partner notification. BV and trichomoniasis look similar (both raise pH, both can smell fishy), but only trichomoniasis (a true STI) triggers partner notification and contact tracing. BV does not.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: Contrast the discharge and pH of BV, trichomoniasis, and candida.
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: BV: thin white/grey, fishy, pH >4.5, minimal itch, NOT an STI. Trichomoniasis: frothy yellow-green, pH >4.5, itchy, IS an STI. Candida: thick white curdy, pH <4.5, prominent itch, NOT an STI.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: Which of BV, trichomoniasis and candida require partner treatment?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: Only trichomoniasis (and other true STIs like chlamydia/gonorrhoea). BV and candida do not require partner treatment.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: What sexual-risk behaviours are associated with BV?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: New sexual partner, multiple partners, unprotected sex, receptive oral sex, douching, and some hygiene practices — all disturb the vaginal flora.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: How does BV interact with HIV risk?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: It increases the risk of ACQUIRING STIs including HIV (raised pH + loss of the lactobacillus barrier), and increases onward HIV transmission risk.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: Besides STI risk, what other complications is BV associated with?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: Post-procedural infection (e.g. after TOP or IUD insertion) and, in pregnancy, adverse outcomes — preterm birth, miscarriage, PROM, chorioamnionitis, low birth weight and postpartum endometritis.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: What are Amsel's criteria for diagnosing BV (need ≥3 of 4)?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: (1) Thin, white, homogenous discharge; (2) vaginal pH >4.5; (3) clue cells on microscopy; (4) positive whiff/amine test (fishy odour with KOH). Diagnose if ≥3 of 4 are present.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: How is BV often diagnosed at the point of care in a GUM clinic?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: With narrow-range pH paper plus microscopy of a wet/Gram-stained slide. The lab equivalent grading is Hay-Ison/Nugent scoring.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: Does asymptomatic BV usually need treatment?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: No — asymptomatic BV usually needs no treatment, except pre-procedure or in pregnancy with risk factors.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: What is the first-line treatment for BV (BASHH)?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 5–7 days. Alternatives: metronidazole 2 g single dose, topical metronidazole gel, or topical clindamycin.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: What key advice must accompany metronidazole treatment?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: Avoid alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction). Also advise avoiding douching, vaginal soaps and shower gels — the key preventive measure.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: What is the key non-drug preventive advice for BV?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: Avoid douching, vaginal soaps and shower gels — these disturb the flora and predispose to recurrence.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: What STI screening should be offered when BV is diagnosed in GUM?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: A full STI screen — BV is a marker of sexual-risk exposure and frequently co-exists with STIs: test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea (NAAT), trichomonas, and offer HIV and syphilis serology.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: Should male partners of a woman with BV be treated?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: No — do NOT treat male partners. Partner treatment does not reduce recurrence. This is the key contrast with true-STI management.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: What is the guidance on female partners of a woman with BV?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: BV is more concordant in women who have sex with women — consider assessment of a female partner, though routine partner treatment is still not recommended.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: How common is recurrence of BV, and how is frequent recurrence managed?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: Recurrence is common (~50–70% within a year). Address modifiable factors and consider suppressive regimens for frequent recurrence.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.front: How is BV managed in pregnancy, and why?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Bacterial Vag.back: Treat symptomatic BV in pregnancy with oral metronidazole (avoid the high-dose single 2 g regimen) because BV is linked to preterm birth, miscarriage, PROM, chorioamnionitis, low birth weight and postpartum endometritis.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: What causes genital warts, and which HPV types are responsible?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: They remain one of the commonest STIs diagnosed in UK sexual health services, though chlamydia, gonorrhoea and genital herpes are diagnosed more often.

Low-risk (HPV 6 & 11): cause ~90% of genital warts, do NOT cause cancer. High-risk (HPV 16 & 18): cause ~70% of cervical cancer (and other anogenital/oropharyngeal cancers), do NOT typically cause warts.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: Which HPV types cause most cervical cancer, and what other cancers does high-risk HPV cause?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: High-risk HPV also causes anal, vulval, vaginal, penile, and oropharyngeal cancers.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: What are the typical clinical features of genital warts?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: Painless lumps on the genital or anal area, either keratinised (hard) or non-keratinised (soft). Often at sites traumatised during intercourse (introitus, penis, perianal skin); single or multiple; may itch, bleed, or cause distress.
Usually a clinical diagnosis based on appearance. Biopsy is reserved for atypical, pigmented, indurated, or otherwise suspicious lesions (to exclude malignancy/intraepithelial neoplasia).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: Why does the keratinised vs non-keratinised distinction matter?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: It guides first-line treatment: soft (non-keratinised) warts respond best to topical podophyllotoxin; hard (keratinised) warts respond best to cryotherapy.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: What is the first-line treatment for multiple, soft (non-keratinised) genital warts?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: Topical podophyllotoxin — patient-applied at home; best for multiple non-keratinised warts.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: What is the first-line treatment for a solitary, hard (keratinised) genital wart?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen) — clinician-applied; best for solitary keratinised warts.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: What are the second-line / resistant-wart treatment options?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: Topical imiquimod (an immune-response modifier) — patient-applied, suitable for keratinised or non-keratinised warts and used if first-line fails or is not tolerated; also trichloroacetic acid, and surgical excision/electrocautery/laser for extensive or recurrent warts. No treatment is clearly superior (BASHH).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: What does BASHH say about choosing a wart treatment?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: No single treatment is superior — choice is guided by wart number/morphology and site plus patient preference, and patients can switch if the response is limited.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: How common is recurrence after treatment of genital warts?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: Recurrence is common (~30%) — warts can recur after apparent clearance, so warn the patient.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: Is partner notification / contact tracing required for genital warts?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: No — formal contact tracing is not required for genital warts, unlike bacterial STIs. Current partners should still be offered assessment and a full STI screen if they wish.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: How is treatment of genital warts modified in pregnancy?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: Podophyllotoxin and imiquimod are contraindicated in pregnancy -> use cryotherapy. Rarely, extensive maternal warts risk neonatal laryngeal (recurrent respiratory) papillomatosis via vertical transmission.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: What additional care should be offered to a patient with genital warts?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: Reassure that types 6 and 11 are not oncogenic, treat the visible warts, encourage HPV vaccination if they are eligible, and continue routine cervical screening — warts themselves do not change cervical screening intervals.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: Which HPV vaccine is used in the UK, and what does it cover?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: A 9-valent HPV vaccine is used — it covers low-risk HPV 6 & 11 (warts) and high-risk 16 & 18 (cancer), plus five more high-risk types (31, 33, 45, 52, 58). It prevents both warts AND HPV-related cancers and pre-cancers.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: Describe the UK routine HPV vaccination programme.
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: Offered to all children in school Year 8 (age 12-13), both boys and girls, as a single dose. Given before sexual debut for maximum benefit.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: Besides the school programme, who else is offered HPV vaccination in the UK?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: Men who have sex with men up to and including age 45 (via sexual health/HIV clinics) — a single dose if under 25, 2 doses if 25 or over. Anyone who missed the school programme can catch up until their 25th birthday. People who are immunosuppressed or living with HIV receive 3 doses.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: Why is HPV vaccination given before sexual debut?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: HPV is acquired soon after first sexual activity; vaccinating beforehand gives maximum protection. High-uptake programmes have dramatically reduced both genital warts and pre-cancerous cervical lesions.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.front: A vaccinated patient asks if they still need cervical screening. What do you advise?
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HPV / Genital.back: Because HPV vaccination prevents the infection that causes almost all cervical cancer, while cervical screening detects changes in those already exposed — the two are complementary, and vaccination does not replace screening. Screening is HPV-primary testing with cytology triage from 25 to 64, 5-yearly if HPV-negative.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: A 27-year-old man presents with dysuria and a scant, clear urethral discharge. Urethral smear microscopy shows 8 polymorphs per high-power field and NO diplococci. What is the diagnosis and most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Gonococcal urethritis — ceftriaxone 1 g IM
Non-gonococcal urethritis — single-dose azithromycin 1 g
Bacterial cystitis — nitrofurantoin
Non-gonococcal urethritis — doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days
No treatment needed
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: Non-gonococcal urethritis — doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: Pus cells (≥5 PMNs/hpf) with no diplococci and a scant mucoid/clear discharge indicate non-gonococcal urethritis. First-line is doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days — preferred over azithromycin because it is more effective against M. genitalium and does not induce macrolide resistance. Gram-negative diplococci would instead point to gonorrhoea.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: A man with urethritis has a urethral smear showing gram-negative intracellular diplococci. How should he be managed?
options: As gonorrhoea — culture for susceptibility, then ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose
As non-gonococcal urethritis, with doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days alone
With reassurance only, as most urethritis settles without treatment
With nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for 7 days, as for a urinary infection
With a single dose of azithromycin 1 g, repeated if symptoms persist
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: As gonorrhoea — culture for susceptibility, then ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci indicate gonococcal urethritis. Take a urethral culture before treating so susceptibilities are available — ceftriaxone-resistant gonorrhoea is emerging — then give ceftriaxone 1 g IM as a single dose. Test for chlamydia and treat if it is detected, and complete a full STI screen. This is the first fork: gonococcal vs non-gonococcal.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: A sample from a man with NGU is positive for Mycoplasma genitalium. Besides treating him, which two additional steps are essential?
options: Repeat the NAAT weekly and treat the partner only if symptomatic
Blood cultures and an ultrasound
Test for macrolide resistance and perform a test of cure after treatment
A test of cure only, with no resistance testing
Nothing further is required
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: Test for macrolide resistance and perform a test of cure after treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: For every M. genitalium-positive sample, test for macrolide resistance (to guide therapy) and perform a test of cure at least 5 weeks after starting treatment, because macrolide resistance is common and rising and an earlier test risks a false positive from residual nucleic acid. This distinguishes M. genitalium management from routine chlamydia care.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: A man with confirmed macrolide-RESISTANT Mycoplasma genitalium urethritis needs treatment. Which is most appropriate?
options: Extended azithromycin (1 g stat then 500 mg OD for 2 days), with a test of cure
Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM as a single dose, with a test of cure
Single-dose azithromycin 1 g, repeated after 2 weeks if still symptomatic
Doxycycline 100 mg BD alone for 7 days, with a test of cure
Moxifloxacin 400 mg OD for 7 days after a doxycycline lead-in, with a test of cure
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: Moxifloxacin 400 mg OD for 7 days after a doxycycline lead-in, with a test of cure
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: Macrolide-resistant M. genitalium is treated with a doxycycline 100 mg BD 7-day lead-in (which reduces organism load) followed by moxifloxacin 400 mg OD for 7 days, then a test of cure at 5 weeks. Macrolide-sensitive infection gets the same doxycycline lead-in followed by extended azithromycin. Single-dose azithromycin would be inappropriate and drives further resistance. Moxifloxacin is a fluoroquinolone, so counsel about tendon rupture, aortic aneurysm/dissection and neuropathy (MHRA).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: A man treated for NGU with doxycycline returns with persistent symptoms and urethritis is reconfirmed on repeat smear. Repeat NAATs are negative for gonorrhoea, chlamydia and M. genitalium, and adherence and reinfection have been excluded. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the same doxycycline 100 mg BD course for a further 7 days
Azithromycin (1 g stat then 500 mg OD ×2) plus metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5 days
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM as a single dose to cover missed gonorrhoea
Reassurance with no further treatment and routine discharge
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for 5 days to cover a urinary cause
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: Azithromycin (1 g stat then 500 mg OD ×2) plus metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: Persistent/recurrent NGU must first be reconfirmed on microscopy, with reinfection, adherence and an untreated partner excluded, and a first-void urine NAAT for M. genitalium with macrolide-resistance testing repeated — M. genitalium accounts for a large share of persistent NGU and macrolide resistance is common, so a positive result would instead direct resistance-guided therapy. Only once M. genitalium is excluded is the empirical regimen after first-line doxycycline extended azithromycin plus metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5 days, covering Trichomonas and anaerobes.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: Which organism is the commonest identifiable cause of non-gonococcal urethritis?
options: Mycoplasma genitalium
Trichomonas vaginalis
Ureaplasma urealyticum
Chlamydia trachomatis
Adenovirus
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis is the commonest identifiable cause of NGU (around a third of cases). M. genitalium is the second commonest and is important because of macrolide resistance; Ureaplasma, Trichomonas, adenovirus and HSV are less common, and many cases are idiopathic.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: Why does BASHH prefer doxycycline over single-dose azithromycin as first-line for NGU?
options: Doxycycline is more effective against M. genitalium and does not induce macrolide resistance
Azithromycin is considerably more expensive than doxycycline
Doxycycline is given as a single dose, which improves adherence
Azithromycin cannot be given orally and must be given by injection
Doxycycline also reliably treats gonorrhoea, so no second drug is needed
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: Doxycycline is more effective against M. genitalium and does not induce macrolide resistance
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: Doxycycline is preferred because it is more effective against M. genitalium than single-dose azithromycin and, crucially, does not induce macrolide resistance — helping preserve macrolide efficacy. Single-dose azithromycin drives resistance and so is avoided; if azithromycin is used, the extended regimen is preferred.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: A urethral smear is used to confirm urethritis. What microscopy finding defines it?
options: Any epithelial cells present
Gram-positive cocci in clusters
≥5 polymorphs (PMNs) per high-power field
Motile trophozoites
Clue cells
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: Urethritis is confirmed on urethral smear by ≥5 polymorphs (PMNs) per high-power field. A first-void urine sediment showing ≥10 polymorphs per high-power field is an accepted alternative. The additional presence of gram-negative intracellular diplococci indicates gonococcal urethritis; their absence with pus cells indicates NGU.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: Which of the following is part of the broader complication spectrum of Mycoplasma genitalium, making it 'chlamydia-like'?
options: It only ever causes urethritis
It causes disseminated gonococcal infection
It causes neurosyphilis
It causes ophthalmia neonatorum specifically
It can cause epididymitis, cervicitis, PID, reactive arthritis and tubal infertility
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: It can cause epididymitis, cervicitis, PID, reactive arthritis and tubal infertility
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: M. genitalium is not just a cause of urethritis — it can also cause epididymitis, cervicitis, endometritis, PID, reactive arthritis, preterm delivery and tubal infertility, mirroring chlamydia's complication profile. This is why it is tested for and treated carefully with resistance-guided therapy.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: A man is diagnosed with NGU. What advice should he be given about sex and partners?
options: He can have sex immediately after taking his first tablet, with no restriction
No sex until treatment is complete (plus 7 days) and partners treated; GUM referral for partner notification
Only condoms are needed, and his partners need no treatment at all
His partners need no assessment, as NGU is not sexually transmissible
He should abstain from sex for 3 months regardless of treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: No sex until treatment is complete (plus 7 days) and partners treated; GUM referral for partner notification
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: He should avoid sex until treatment is complete (and for 7 days after) and until partners have been treated, to prevent reinfection and transmission. GUM referral for partner notification/contact tracing and a full STI screen (HIV, syphilis) are standard.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: A man presents with urethritis but NAATs are negative for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and M. genitalium, and there is no Trichomonas. He has ≥5 PMNs on smear. How is this best described and managed?
options: He does not have urethritis, as no organism has been identified
He needs no treatment at all, as the NAATs were all negative
Gonococcal urethritis — give ceftriaxone 1 g IM as a single dose
Idiopathic/non-specific NGU — treat empirically as NGU (doxycycline) with GUM follow-up
Recurrent syphilis presenting with urethral inflammation
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: Idiopathic/non-specific NGU — treat empirically as NGU (doxycycline) with GUM follow-up
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: A significant proportion of NGU is idiopathic (no pathogen identified), yet the smear confirms urethritis (≥5 PMNs/hpf). It is still treated empirically as NGU with doxycycline, alongside partner management, STI screen and GUM follow-up. Persistence would trigger the recurrent-NGU pathway.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: Why must macrolide-resistance testing be prioritised for M. genitalium specifically?
options: Because macrolide resistance is common and rising, so it determines whether azithromycin or moxifloxacin is used
Because M. genitalium is untreatable once resistance has developed
Because M. genitalium never responds to antibiotic treatment of any kind
Because M. genitalium is not sexually transmitted and needs no partner work
Because M. genitalium only affects women, so men need no resistance testing
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: Because macrolide resistance is common and rising, so it determines whether azithromycin or moxifloxacin is used
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: Macrolide resistance in M. genitalium is common and increasing, so resistance testing directs treatment: after a doxycycline lead-in, macrolide-sensitive infection is treated with extended azithromycin, whereas resistant infection requires moxifloxacin 400 mg OD for 7 days. A test of cure at 5 weeks is performed in all cases.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: A 24-year-old man with NGU is found to have Trichomonas vaginalis contributing to persistent symptoms. Which drug specifically covers this in the recurrent-NGU regimens?
options: Doxycycline
Ceftriaxone
Metronidazole
Moxifloxacin
Azithromycin
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: Metronidazole is added in recurrent NGU regimens to cover Trichomonas vaginalis and anaerobes. Moxifloxacin covers macrolide-resistant M. genitalium; the combination chosen depends on what was used first-line.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: Which statement about the presentation of urethritis is correct?
options: It is always symptomatic
Symptoms only occur in women
It always causes profuse green discharge
It never causes discharge
It presents with dysuria and/or urethral discharge, but can also be asymptomatic
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: It presents with dysuria and/or urethral discharge, but can also be asymptomatic
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: Urethritis typically presents with dysuria and/or urethral discharge, but a substantial number of cases are asymptomatic — which supports testing at-risk individuals. Profuse green/yellow discharge suggests a gonococcal cause, whereas scant mucoid discharge suggests NGU.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.question: A man completes treatment for macrolide-sensitive M. genitalium urethritis. What is the correct follow-up?
options: No follow-up is needed once the course has been completed
A test of cure at least 5 weeks after starting treatment, as for all M. genitalium infections
Automatically repeat the same treatment course after 6 weeks
Re-test only if his partner develops symptoms in the next 6 weeks
Lifelong suppressive doxycycline 100 mg once daily
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.answer: A test of cure at least 5 weeks after starting treatment, as for all M. genitalium infections
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethritis (N.explanation: A test of cure is recommended for all M. genitalium infections, taken at least 5 weeks after treatment starts — earlier testing risks a false positive from residual nucleic acid. This applies whether the isolate was macrolide-sensitive (doxycycline lead-in then extended azithromycin) or resistant (doxycycline lead-in then moxifloxacin).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A 28-year-old man presents with a single, PAINLESS, indurated ulcer on his penis and non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Genital herpes
Behçet's disease
Chancroid
Primary syphilis (chancre)
Lymphogranuloma venereum secondary stage
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Primary syphilis (chancre)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: A single, painless, indurated genital ulcer (chancre) with painless local lymphadenopathy is classic for primary syphilis. The painlessness is the key discriminator: herpes and chancroid (H. ducreyi) cause painful ulcers. Dark-field microscopy/PCR of the lesion and serology confirm it.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A 30-year-old woman has a maculopapular rash involving her trunk, palms and soles, with moist wart-like plaques around the vulva and mouth ulcers. What stage of syphilis does this represent?
options: Secondary syphilis
Primary syphilis
Early latent syphilis
Tertiary syphilis
Congenital syphilis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Secondary syphilis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: A rash involving the palms and soles, with condylomata lata (moist grey wart-like plaques) and snail-track mouth ulcers, is classic secondary syphilis (~6–10 weeks), a disseminated systemic stage. A rash on the palms and soles is a strong pointer to secondary syphilis (or other specific causes).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A patient with neurosyphilis is found to have a small, irregular pupil that constricts on accommodation but does not react to light. What is this sign called?
options: Marcus Gunn pupil
Holmes-Adie pupil
Argyll-Robertson pupil
Horner's pupil
Hutchinson's pupil
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Argyll-Robertson pupil
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: The Argyll-Robertson pupil — small and irregular, constricting on accommodation but not reacting to light — is a classic sign of neurosyphilis. It is usually bilateral, and reflects neurological involvement that can occur at any stage of infection.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: Which treatment is first-line for early syphilis (primary, secondary or early latent) in a patient with no penicillin allergy?
options: Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 doses
Azithromycin 1 g single dose
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM as a single dose
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM as a single dose
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent) is treated with a single dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM. Late latent/tertiary disease needs 3 weekly doses (the organism divides slowly), and neurosyphilis needs procaine or IV benzylpenicillin — benzathine does not reach the CSF. Doxycycline is the alternative only in penicillin allergy.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A pregnant woman with primary syphilis reports a severe penicillin allergy. What is the correct management?
options: Treat with doxycycline for 14 days
Desensitise to penicillin and treat with penicillin, as it is essential in pregnancy
Use azithromycin as a safe alternative
Delay treatment until after delivery
Treat with ceftriaxone only and avoid penicillin
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Desensitise to penicillin and treat with penicillin, as it is essential in pregnancy
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Penicillin is essential to prevent congenital syphilis and is the only reliably effective treatment in pregnancy, so a penicillin-allergic pregnant woman should be desensitised and treated with penicillin. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy, and macrolides are no longer recommended due to resistance.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A few hours after his first penicillin injection for syphilis, a patient develops fever, rash, tachycardia, headache and myalgia, which settle within a day. What has occurred?
options: Anaphylaxis to penicillin
Septic shock
Serum sickness
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
Drug-induced lupus
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute, self-limiting febrile reaction within hours of the first antibiotic dose, caused by cytokine release as spirochaetes are killed en masse. It is NOT an allergy — manage with antipyretics. It can be dangerous in pregnancy (contractions/fetal distress) or neuro/cardiovascular syphilis (use steroid cover).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A patient treated for syphilis 1 year ago has a persistently positive treponemal (TPPA) test but a non-treponemal (RPR) titre that has fallen fourfold. How should this be interpreted?
options: Treatment has worked — treponemal tests stay positive for life; the falling RPR shows response
Treatment has failed and he needs re-treating
He has been reinfected since treatment
He has developed neurosyphilis
The tests are contradictory and unreliable
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Treatment has worked — treponemal tests stay positive for life; the falling RPR shows response
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Treponemal tests (EIA/TPPA) remain positive for life even after cure, so they cannot indicate cure. The non-treponemal RPR/VDRL titre tracks disease activity: a falling titre indicates successful treatment, whereas a rising titre would suggest active disease or reinfection.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: An 8-year-old child has notched, peg-shaped permanent upper incisors, interstitial keratitis and sensorineural deafness. What condition and eponymous triad does this represent?
options: Congenital rubella; Gregg's triad
Congenital toxoplasmosis; Sabin triad
Congenital syphilis; Hutchinson's triad
Congenital CMV; classic triad
Fetal alcohol syndrome
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Congenital syphilis; Hutchinson's triad
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Congenital syphilis classically causes Hutchinson's triad: Hutchinson's teeth (notched, peg-shaped permanent incisors) + interstitial keratitis + sensorineural deafness. These are LATE stigmata, appearing from about 5-10 years, not at birth — early congenital syphilis in the first weeks presents with snuffles, a rash often on palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly and jaundice. It is prevented by offering all pregnant women syphilis serology at booking and treating with penicillin.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: Which investigation directly detects Treponema pallidum from a genital ulcer?
options: Blood culture
Urine NAAT
Gram stain of the ulcer
RPR titre alone
Dark-field microscopy and/or PCR of a swab from the lesion
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Dark-field microscopy and/or PCR of a swab from the lesion
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: T. pallidum cannot be routinely cultured, so direct detection is by dark-field microscopy and/or PCR of a swab taken from the chancre/lesion. Serology (treponemal + non-treponemal) is the mainstay for screening/staging and monitoring, but direct tests confirm the organism in an active lesion.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A patient's non-treponemal (RPR) test is positive but the confirmatory treponemal test is negative. She is pregnant and has a history of SLE. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Active syphilis requiring immediate treatment
A biological false-positive RPR (e.g. from pregnancy or SLE/antiphospholipid)
Neurosyphilis
Congenital syphilis
Laboratory error that can be ignored
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: A biological false-positive RPR (e.g. from pregnancy or SLE/antiphospholipid)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Non-treponemal tests (RPR/VDRL) are sensitive but non-specific and can give biological false positives in pregnancy, SLE/antiphospholipid syndrome and other infections. Because the specific treponemal test is negative, active syphilis is not confirmed. This is exactly why a positive RPR is always confirmed with a treponemal test.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A man is diagnosed with late latent syphilis (>2 years, asymptomatic, positive serology). He has no penicillin allergy. What is the appropriate treatment?
options: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose
A single oral dose of azithromycin 2 g
Doxycycline for 7 days
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 doses
No treatment as late latent is non-infectious
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 doses
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Late latent (and tertiary non-neuro) syphilis requires benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 doses — a longer course than early syphilis because the organism divides slowly. Even though late latent is not sexually infectious, it still requires treatment to prevent progression and vertical transmission.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A patient with syphilis develops chest imaging showing an ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm and a murmur of aortic regurgitation. Which stage/complication does this indicate?
options: Cardiovascular tertiary syphilis (syphilitic aortitis)
Primary syphilis
Secondary syphilis
Early latent syphilis
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Cardiovascular tertiary syphilis (syphilitic aortitis)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Cardiovascular syphilis is a tertiary complication in which aortitis affects the ascending aorta, causing a thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic regurgitation. It occurs years after untreated infection, alongside gummas and neurosyphilis as the tertiary triad.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a syphilitic chancre from chancroid and herpes?
options: The syphilitic chancre is painful; herpes and chancroid are painless
All three cause painful ulcers
The syphilitic chancre is painless and indurated; herpes and chancroid cause painful ulcers
All three cause painless ulcers
Only chancroid is painless
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: The syphilitic chancre is painless and indurated; herpes and chancroid cause painful ulcers
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: The syphilitic chancre is characteristically painless and indurated, whereas chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) and genital herpes produce painful ulcers. This pain distinction is a classic exam discriminator: a painless genital ulcer should prompt consideration of syphilis.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A patient with suspected neurosyphilis needs confirmatory investigation. What is the most appropriate test?
options: Repeat serum RPR only
Dark-field microscopy of blood
MRI spine alone
Nerve conduction studies
Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis (VDRL, protein, cells)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis (VDRL, protein, cells)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Neurosyphilis is investigated with a lumbar puncture, examining the CSF for VDRL, raised protein and a cell count (pleocytosis). Treatment is with IV/procaine penicillin for ~14 days with steroid cover, differing from the IM regimens used for non-neurological disease.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A patient found to have syphilis on screening asks what else should be done besides treatment. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: No further action is needed once she has been treated
GUM referral, partner notification, a full STI screen including HIV, and follow-up serology
Only a repeat RPR test in five years time
Treat the partner only if he becomes symptomatic
Immediate hospital admission for all cases
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: GUM referral, partner notification, a full STI screen including HIV, and follow-up serology
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Syphilis management includes GUM referral, partner notification/contact tracing (look-back varies by stage), a full STI screen (HIV co-infection is common), abstaining from sex until lesions have healed and at least 2 weeks after treatment finishes, and follow-up serology at 3, 6 and 12 months looking for a fourfold fall in RPR/VDRL.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A pregnant woman is being treated for syphilis with penicillin. Why is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction a particular concern in her case, and how is the risk mitigated?
options: It causes permanent penicillin allergy; give antihistamines
It requires stopping penicillin immediately and switching to doxycycline
It is harmless in pregnancy and needs no attention
It may trigger uterine contractions and fetal distress; treat without delay with monitoring and antipyretics
It only affects the tertiary stage
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: It may trigger uterine contractions and fetal distress; treat without delay with monitoring and antipyretics
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: In pregnancy the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can precipitate uterine contractions and fetal distress, so women are warned, given antipyretics and fluids, and monitored — but treatment is never delayed, because untreated syphilis risks congenital infection and stillbirth. Steroids are NOT recommended to prevent it in pregnancy; steroid cover is reserved for cardiovascular and neurosyphilis. It is not an allergy, so penicillin is continued.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: Which statement about early versus late latent syphilis is correct regarding infectivity?
options: Early latent is potentially sexually infectious; late latent is not, but can still transmit vertically
Both early and late latent are highly sexually infectious
Late latent is more sexually infectious than early latent
Neither early nor late latent can transmit vertically
Only late latent syphilis can be treated with penicillin
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Early latent is potentially sexually infectious; late latent is not, but can still transmit vertically
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Early latent syphilis (<2 years) is potentially sexually infectious, whereas late latent (>2 years) is not sexually infectious but can still be transmitted vertically to a fetus — which is why latent syphilis in pregnancy still requires treatment.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A patient allergic to penicillin (not pregnant) is diagnosed with early syphilis. Which is the most appropriate alternative treatment?
options: Azithromycin 1 g single dose
Benzathine penicillin after antihistamine pre-treatment
Doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 14 days
Metronidazole for 14 days
No treatment is possible
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 14 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: In a non-pregnant penicillin-allergic patient, doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days (28 days if late) is the recommended alternative (ceftriaxone is another option), though it does not cover neurosyphilis. Macrolides such as azithromycin are no longer recommended because of resistance. In pregnancy, penicillin desensitisation would be required instead.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: A patient completes treatment for secondary syphilis. Over the following months, which serological change best confirms successful treatment?
options: The treponemal (TPPA) test becomes negative
The dark-field microscopy becomes positive
A rise in the RPR titre
No change in any test
A significant fall (e.g. fourfold) in the non-treponemal (RPR/VDRL) titre
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: A significant fall (e.g. fourfold) in the non-treponemal (RPR/VDRL) titre
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Successful treatment is confirmed by a significant fall in the non-treponemal RPR/VDRL titre (typically fourfold), as these track disease activity. Treponemal tests remain positive for life and so do not revert to negative; a rising RPR would instead indicate treatment failure or reinfection.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.question: Which of the following is a recognised feature of tabes dorsalis in neurosyphilis?
options: Spastic paraparesis with brisk reflexes
Sensory ataxia, lightning pains and loss of proprioception from dorsal column degeneration
Resting tremor and bradykinesia
Bilateral facial weakness
Cerebellar intention tremor
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.answer: Sensory ataxia, lightning pains and loss of proprioception from dorsal column degeneration
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Syphilis.explanation: Tabes dorsalis results from dorsal column degeneration, causing sensory ataxia, lightning (shooting) pains, and loss of proprioception/vibration sense. It is one of the classic neurosyphilis syndromes, along with general paresis (dementia) and the Argyll-Robertson pupil.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: A 30-year-old man presents with intense generalised itch that is much worse at night, with thin wavy grey lines in his finger web spaces. His partner is also itchy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Atopic eczema
Urticaria
Contact dermatitis
Scabies
Psoriasis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Intense itch worse at night, pathognomonic burrows in the finger webs, and an itchy contact (partner) are classic for scabies. Household/partner clustering is a strong clue, and the burrow (thin wavy grey line) is the diagnostic sign. It can be sexually transmitted, warranting consideration of an STI screen.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: A patient is diagnosed with classic scabies and prescribed permethrin 5% cream. Which instruction is most important for successful treatment?
options: Apply to the whole body from the neck down, leave 8–12 hours, and REPEAT the whole application after 7 days
Apply only to the visibly affected areas once
Apply for 30 minutes then wash off, once only
Apply only to the hands and genitals
Take it as an oral tablet
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Apply to the whole body from the neck down, leave 8–12 hours, and REPEAT the whole application after 7 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Permethrin must be applied to the whole body from the neck down (including webs, under nails, genitals, soles), left on 8–12 hours, and — crucially — repeated after 7 days to kill newly hatched mites (eggs survive the first dose). Omitting the second application is the commonest cause of apparent treatment failure.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: A woman treated for scabies 10 days ago returns because she is still itchy, though she followed the treatment correctly and has no new burrows. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The treatment has failed and needs a different drug
She has developed crusted scabies
Post-scabetic itch — the hypersensitivity reaction persists for 2–6 weeks after successful treatment
She was never infested
She needs oral antibiotics
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Post-scabetic itch — the hypersensitivity reaction persists for 2–6 weeks after successful treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Itch is a hypersensitivity reaction that outlasts the dead mites, persisting 2–6 weeks after successful treatment (post-scabetic itch) — this is NOT treatment failure. Manage with emollients, a mild topical steroid and a non-sedating antihistamine, and reassure. New burrows or spreading lesions would suggest true failure/reinfestation.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: A frail elderly nursing-home resident on long-term steroids develops thick, hyperkeratotic, warty crusts with relatively little itch, and several staff have become itchy. What is the diagnosis and the key management priority?
options: Psoriasis — topical steroids
Seborrhoeic dermatitis — antifungal shampoo
Eczema — emollients only
Classic scabies — single permethrin application
Crusted (Norwegian) scabies — isolate, treat with topical scabicide plus oral ivermectin, and screen contacts
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies — isolate, treat with topical scabicide plus oral ivermectin, and screen contacts
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies occurs in the immunocompromised/frail, with thousands–millions of mites producing hyperkeratotic crusts and often little itch. It is extremely contagious (explaining the staff outbreak), so management requires isolation, aggressive treatment (topical scabicide + repeated oral ivermectin) and contact screening — a public-health emergency.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: Which single step is most important to prevent 'ping-pong' reinfestation in a household with scabies?
options: Treat only symptomatic family members
Treat all household members, sexual partners and close contacts simultaneously, even if asymptomatic
Isolate the index case for 6 weeks
Repeat the index case's treatment weekly for a month
Avoid washing any bedding
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Treat all household members, sexual partners and close contacts simultaneously, even if asymptomatic
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Because there is a pre-symptomatic window (first infestation takes 4–6 weeks to itch), all household members, sexual partners and close skin contacts must be treated at the SAME TIME, even if asymptomatic, to prevent reinfestation. Decontaminating bedding/clothing (hot wash or bag for 72 h) supports this.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: Why does the itch of a FIRST scabies infestation take 4–6 weeks to develop, whereas re-infestation itches within days?
options: The mites multiply faster the second time
Re-infestation always involves crusted scabies
The second infestation involves a different mite species
The itch is a hypersensitivity reaction — the first infestation must sensitise the immune system (4–6 weeks), but on re-infestation the immune system is already primed
Antihistamines change the timing
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: The itch is a hypersensitivity reaction — the first infestation must sensitise the immune system (4–6 weeks), but on re-infestation the immune system is already primed
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Scabies itch is a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction to the mite/eggs/faeces. A first infestation needs 4–6 weeks to sensitise the immune system before itch appears, while a re-infestation provokes itch within 1–3 days because the immune system is already primed.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: A pregnant woman with classic scabies needs treatment. Which option is appropriate and which should be avoided?
options: Permethrin 5% cream is appropriate; oral ivermectin is not licensed in pregnancy
Oral ivermectin is first-line in pregnancy
No treatment is safe in pregnancy
Malathion is contraindicated but ivermectin is fine
Only antihistamines should be used
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Permethrin 5% cream is appropriate; oral ivermectin is not licensed in pregnancy
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Permethrin 5% cream is the appropriate first-line treatment and is used in pregnancy. Oral ivermectin is not licensed in pregnancy (or for those under 15 kg), so it is avoided. Malathion is a topical alternative if permethrin is unsuitable.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: A child with scabies is scratching heavily and develops honey-coloured crusted lesions with surrounding erythema. What complication has occurred?
options: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies
Nodular scabies
Secondary bacterial infection (impetiginisation) with Staphylococcus/Streptococcus
Post-scabetic itch
Contact dermatitis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Scratching can cause secondary bacterial infection (impetiginisation) with Staph/Strep, producing honey-coloured crusts — which in endemic settings can lead to post-streptococcal complications (glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever). This requires antibiotics in addition to scabies treatment.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: When applying permethrin to an INFANT with scabies, how does the application differ from an adult?
options: It should not be used in infants at all
Oral ivermectin is used instead
Only the trunk is treated
It is applied for only 1 hour
The head, face and scalp should also be treated (avoiding the eyes), unlike in adults where it is neck-down
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: The head, face and scalp should also be treated (avoiding the eyes), unlike in adults where it is neck-down
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: In adults, permethrin is applied from the neck down. In infants, the elderly and the immunocompromised, the head, face and scalp are also treated (avoiding the eyes) because scabies can involve these areas in these groups. The 8–12 hour duration and 7-day repeat still apply.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: A patient asks how to decontaminate their home after scabies treatment. What is the correct advice?
options: No decontamination is needed
Wash clothing, bedding and towels at ≥50–60°C and/or seal items in a bag for 72 hours
Fumigate the whole house with insecticide
Discard all furniture
Freeze all bedding for 24 hours
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Wash clothing, bedding and towels at ≥50–60°C and/or seal items in a bag for 72 hours
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Mites die off-host within about 3 days, so clothing/bedding/towels should be hot-washed (≥50–60°C) and/or sealed in a bag for 72 hours. Extensive fumigation or discarding furniture is unnecessary; this is a minor route in classic scabies (major in crusted).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: Which statement about the diagnosis of scabies is correct?
options: A negative skin scraping reliably excludes scabies
Patch testing is the gold standard
A blood test confirms scabies
Diagnosis is largely clinical (itch, burrows, distribution, affected contacts); microscopy has low sensitivity so a negative result does not exclude it
Only a biopsy can diagnose scabies
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Diagnosis is largely clinical (itch, burrows, distribution, affected contacts); microscopy has low sensitivity so a negative result does not exclude it
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Scabies is largely a clinical diagnosis based on itch, burrows, typical distribution and affected contacts. Skin scraping microscopy (mites/eggs/faecal pellets) confirms it but has low sensitivity, so a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis. Dermoscopy may show the 'delta-wing jet' sign.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: A man treated for scabies has persistent itchy nodules on the scrotum and groin weeks after successful treatment, with no new burrows. What is this most likely to be?
options: Nodular scabies — persistent hypersensitivity nodules that can outlast treatment
Treatment failure requiring a new scabicide
Genital warts
Molluscum contagiosum
Secondary syphilis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Nodular scabies — persistent hypersensitivity nodules that can outlast treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Nodular scabies describes persistent itchy nodules (often on the genitals/groin) that represent an ongoing hypersensitivity reaction and can outlast successful treatment. They are managed with topical steroids and reassurance rather than repeated scabicide, provided there is no evidence of active infestation.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: A sexually active adult is diagnosed with genital scabies at a GUM clinic. Besides treating the scabies, what is appropriate?
options: No further action
Immediate hospital admission
Consider a full STI screen and treat sexual contacts, as scabies can be a marker of sexual-risk exposure
Lifelong permethrin prophylaxis
Contact tracing is never needed for scabies
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Consider a full STI screen and treat sexual contacts, as scabies can be a marker of sexual-risk exposure
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Scabies can be sexually transmitted, so a case presenting to GUM warrants consideration of a full STI screen and treatment of sexual contacts (as a marker of sexual-risk exposure), in addition to treating the scabies itself and close household contacts simultaneously.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: Which feature would most suggest CRUSTED rather than classic scabies?
options: A few burrows with intense nocturnal itch
Nodules on the scrotum
Itch confined to the finger webs
A single itchy household member
Thick hyperkeratotic warty crusts with a very high mite burden and often minimal itch
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Thick hyperkeratotic warty crusts with a very high mite burden and often minimal itch
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies is characterised by thick, hyperkeratotic, warty crusts teeming with thousands to millions of mites, with itch that may be mild or absent — quite different from classic scabies (a few mites, prominent nocturnal itch, discrete burrows). Its extreme contagiousness makes recognition critical.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: A patient with scabies is prescribed permethrin and washes their hands with soap 4 hours into the 8–12 hour application window. What should they do?
options: Restart the entire application immediately
Reapply permethrin to the hands, as the cream must remain in contact for the full window
Wash it all off and try again next week
Nothing — hand washing does not matter
Switch to oral ivermectin
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Reapply permethrin to the hands, as the cream must remain in contact for the full window
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Permethrin must stay in contact with the skin for the full 8–12 hours, so if the hands are washed during the window the cream should be reapplied to them. This attention to technique (plus the 7-day repeat and treating contacts) is what determines treatment success.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.question: Which of the following best explains why treating scabies is often perceived to 'fail' despite the correct drug?
options: Permethrin is intrinsically ineffective
Scabies cannot be cured
The mite is resistant to all treatments
Failure is almost always a technique or contact problem — e.g. omitting the 7-day repeat, incomplete application, or untreated contacts — rather than drug failure
Antihistamines block the scabicide
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.answer: Failure is almost always a technique or contact problem — e.g. omitting the 7-day repeat, incomplete application, or untreated contacts — rather than drug failure
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Scabies.explanation: Apparent scabies treatment failure is almost always due to technique or contact issues — most commonly omitting the essential second application at 7 days, applying the cream incompletely, or failing to treat all close contacts simultaneously (leading to reinfestation) — rather than genuine drug failure.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: A 23-year-old woman attends the GUM clinic with bilateral lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia and abnormal bleeding. On examination she has cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness. What is the single most important initial investigation?
options: Pelvic ultrasound
Diagnostic laparoscopy
CRP and ESR
A pregnancy test (β-hCG) to exclude ectopic pregnancy
Endometrial biopsy
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: A pregnancy test (β-hCG) to exclude ectopic pregnancy
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: A β-hCG must always be done first in suspected PID to exclude an ectopic pregnancy, which can present similarly and is life-threatening — cervical motion tenderness occurs in ectopic pregnancy too, and appendicitis is the other major mimic. A positive test also changes treatment: doxycycline and quinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy, and PID in pregnancy warrants admission for parenteral therapy.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: A woman with suspected PID has NAAT swabs sent but results will take time. Her clinical picture is consistent with PID. What is the correct management approach?
options: Start empirical antibiotics now — PID is a clinical diagnosis and delay risks infertility
Wait for the swab results before starting any antibiotics
Give analgesia only and review her again in a week's time
Treat only if the pregnancy test comes back positive
Admit for laparoscopy before starting any treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: Start empirical antibiotics now — PID is a clinical diagnosis and delay risks infertility
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: PID is a clinical diagnosis and a negative or pending swab does not exclude it. Because the complications of delay (infertility, ectopic, chronic pain) are serious, there should be a low threshold to start empirical treatment on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for results.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: Which is the first-line antibiotic regimen for outpatient PID according to BASHH?
options: Oral doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days alone, with no other antibiotic cover
Oral azithromycin 1 g as a single dose alone, with no other antibiotic cover
IM ceftriaxone 1 g single dose + oral doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days + oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days
Oral ofloxacin 400 mg BD for 14 days as the routine first-choice regimen
IM ceftriaxone 1 g as a single dose alone, with no oral antibiotic follow-on
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: IM ceftriaxone 1 g single dose + oral doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days + oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: First-line outpatient treatment is IM ceftriaxone 1 g (covering gonorrhoea) + doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days (chlamydia) + metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days (anaerobes). Single-agent regimens are inadequate for the polymicrobial nature of PID. Doxycycline does not reliably clear Mycoplasma genitalium, which needs specific cover if identified. Ofloxacin-based therapy is now second-line (MHRA).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: Why are quinolone-based regimens (e.g. ofloxacin) now second-line for PID?
options: They are ineffective against anaerobes, which are the main organisms in PID
They only cover chlamydia and have no activity against anything else
They cannot be given orally and must always be given intravenously
They are contraindicated in all women of reproductive age without exception
Because of MHRA fluoroquinolone safety advice, and they are avoided if gonococcal PID is likely
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: Because of MHRA fluoroquinolone safety advice, and they are avoided if gonococcal PID is likely
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: Following MHRA fluoroquinolone safety advice (tendon/neuro/QT risks), quinolones such as ofloxacin are now second-line for PID, and they should be avoided where gonococcal PID is likely because of gonococcal quinolone resistance.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: A woman is treated for PID. What is the defining sexual-health step that distinguishes GUM management?
options: Arranging a follow-up cervical smear before any other action
GUM referral with partner notification and empirical treatment of partners, with no sex until both are treated
Starting the combined oral contraceptive pill to prevent further episodes of PID
Removing her intrauterine device in all cases before treatment
A repeat pregnancy test in 2 weeks with no other follow-up
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: GUM referral with partner notification and empirical treatment of partners, with no sex until both are treated
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: The defining GUM step is partner notification/contact tracing: current and recent partners (look back ~6 months) should be assessed, tested and treated empirically (usually chlamydia/gonorrhoea) to prevent 'ping-pong' reinfection, with no sex until the patient and partner(s) have completed treatment.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: Microscopy of a vaginal smear from a woman with lower abdominal pain shows NO pus cells. How does this affect the likelihood of PID?
options: It confirms PID
It confirms gonococcal PID specifically
It has no diagnostic value
It makes PID unlikely — a useful rule-out
It indicates a tubo-ovarian abscess
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: It makes PID unlikely — a useful rule-out
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: The absence of pus cells on microscopy makes PID unlikely and is a useful rule-out test. Their presence is non-specific but supports inflammation. It does not override a convincing clinical picture, and it says nothing about the surgical differentials — ectopic pregnancy and appendicitis still have to be excluded. PID remains a clinical diagnosis.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: Which organism is the commonest cause of PID and often causes it to be the first sign of infection?
options: Chlamydia trachomatis
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Mycoplasma genitalium
Gardnerella vaginalis
Trichomonas vaginalis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis is the commonest cause of PID and is often silent, so PID may be the first manifestation of infection. Gonorrhoea causes more severe PID and drives the ceftriaxone-based regimen; Mycoplasma genitalium is increasingly recognised.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: A woman with a copper IUD develops mild PID. What is the correct advice regarding her device?
options: Remove the IUD immediately in all cases
The IUD must be replaced with a hormonal one
In mild PID the IUD can usually be left in situ
The IUD guarantees the PID will not respond to treatment
Remove it and avoid all contraception for 6 months
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: In mild PID the IUD can usually be left in situ
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: In mild-to-moderate PID the intrauterine device can usually be left in situ while treating, provided she is improving by 48-72 hours. Removal is considered if there is no clinical improvement or the PID is severe — and if the device is removed, consider emergency contraception where there has been unprotected sex in the preceding 7 days. Antibiotic treatment and partner management proceed regardless.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: A woman treated empirically for PID returns at 72 hours with no improvement and worsening pain and swinging fevers. What complication should be considered?
options: Simple reinfection
Endometriosis
Ovarian cyst rupture
Ovarian torsion
Tubo-ovarian abscess, which may require admission and drainage
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: Tubo-ovarian abscess, which may require admission and drainage
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: Failure to improve by ~72 hours should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis and assessment for a tubo-ovarian abscess, which may require admission, imaging and drainage. This scheduled review is a built-in safety net of PID management.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: A 25-year-old woman has had two previous episodes of PID and now wishes to conceive. Which complication is she most at risk of, and why does this matter?
options: Endometrial cancer arising from chronic inflammation of the uterus
Tubal factor infertility and ectopic pregnancy, because tubal damage accumulates with each PID episode
Cervical incompetence causing recurrent second-trimester loss
Epithelial ovarian cancer presenting years later with ascites
Uterine fibroids growing in response to repeated infection
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: Tubal factor infertility and ectopic pregnancy, because tubal damage accumulates with each PID episode
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: Each episode of PID increases the risk of tubal damage, leading to tubal factor infertility and ectopic pregnancy from tubal scarring. This cumulative risk is a key reason for treating STIs early and having a low threshold for empirical PID treatment.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: A patient with PID also reports right upper quadrant pain. Perihepatitis is suspected. What is this complication and its typical cause?
options: Cholecystitis from gallstones, with a positive Murphy's sign on examination
Budd-Chiari syndrome from hepatic venous outflow obstruction
A hepatitis B flare causing right upper quadrant tenderness
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome — perihepatitis with 'violin-string' adhesions from ascending infection
A subphrenic abscess following an unrecognised bowel perforation
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome — perihepatitis with 'violin-string' adhesions from ascending infection
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatitis (inflammation of the liver capsule with 'violin-string' adhesions) caused by ascending chlamydial or gonococcal infection, presenting with RUQ pain alongside PID. It is a classic examinable complication.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: A woman's PID swabs return negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. She had already started empirical treatment. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Continue treatment — a negative STI test does not exclude PID, which is often polymicrobial
Stop the antibiotics immediately, as a negative STI screen excludes PID
Switch to a single-agent antibiotic now that the screen is negative
The diagnosis must have been wrong, so investigate for another cause
Only continue treatment if a repeat swab in a week is positive
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: Continue treatment — a negative STI test does not exclude PID, which is often polymicrobial
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: Gonorrhoea or chlamydia are identified in up to a quarter of UK PID cases, but a negative STI test does NOT exclude PID because many cases are polymicrobial or test-negative. Empirical treatment started on clinical suspicion should be completed.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: Which additional serological tests should be offered to a woman diagnosed with PID, reflecting its sexual-health significance?
options: Thyroid function tests
Serum CA-125
HIV and syphilis serology as part of a full STI screen
Rheumatoid factor
Serum ferritin
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: HIV and syphilis serology as part of a full STI screen
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: Because PID signals sexual-risk exposure and STI coinfection is common, a full STI screen including HIV and syphilis serology should be offered alongside the NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhoea. This is central to the GUM approach.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: A woman with PID is found on testing to have Mycoplasma genitalium. How might this affect treatment?
options: No change is needed
It means the PID is not sexually acquired
She needs only metronidazole
It confirms she does not need partner treatment
Specific cover with moxifloxacin may be required
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: Specific cover with moxifloxacin may be required
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: Mycoplasma genitalium is an increasingly recognised cause of PID and may require specific antimicrobial cover with moxifloxacin, particularly if standard treatment fails or resistance is identified. Partner management still applies.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: Which examination finding is the classic sign of PID?
options: A palpable pelvic mass
Cervical motion tenderness ('cervical excitation')
Abdominal guarding in the right iliac fossa only
A fixed retroverted uterus
Vulval ulceration
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: Cervical motion tenderness (cervical excitation) is the classic sign of PID, reflecting inflammation of the pelvic organs, and is typically accompanied by adnexal/pelvic tenderness and cervicitis. It also features in ectopic pregnancy, which is why β-hCG is mandatory.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.question: Why are PID and STI screening described as 'inseparable' in the GUM setting?
options: Because PID is never caused by sexually transmitted infections, so screening is irrelevant
Because PID only ever occurs in women who have already been screened and treated for STIs
Because a full STI screen replaces the need to treat PID with antibiotics at all
Because PID is caused by the same STIs that screening detects, so it triggers full screening and partner management
Because screening itself cures PID, so no further antibiotic treatment is needed
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.answer: Because PID is caused by the same STIs that screening detects, so it triggers full screening and partner management
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__PID (SH frami.explanation: PID is caused by the same organisms (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, Mycoplasma genitalium) that GUM clinics screen for, so a diagnosis of PID mandates full STI screening and partner notification, and conversely early STI detection/treatment prevents PID — making the two inseparable.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A 22-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of multiple painful genital ulcers, fever, malaise and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, and dysuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Primary syphilis (chancre)
Lymphogranuloma venereum
Bacterial vaginosis
Primary genital herpes
