Vulval candidiasis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: Multiple PAINFUL genital ulcers with systemic symptoms (fever, malaise) and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy are classic for a PRIMARY genital herpes episode, which is more severe than recurrences. A syphilitic chancre is typically single and painless; LGV's primary ulcer is painless; candida causes itch not ulcers.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A woman with suspected first-episode genital herpes attends. What is the gold-standard investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: NAAT (HSV PCR) of a swab from the lesion base
Serum HSV IgG
Tzanck smear alone
Dark-field microscopy
High vaginal swab for culture
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: NAAT (HSV PCR) of a swab from the lesion base
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: NAAT (HSV PCR) from a swab of the lesion base is the gold standard and also types HSV-1 vs HSV-2. Serology is reserved for recurrent ulceration of unknown cause or to determine primary vs recurrent infection in pregnancy. Tzanck smear is non-specific; dark-field is for syphilis.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A 25-year-old man presents within 3 days of onset of his first episode of genital herpes with new lesions still forming. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Topical aciclovir cream only
A single dose of oral azithromycin
Oral aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days
Oral aciclovir 400 mg twice daily for 6 months
Intravenous aciclovir
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Oral aciclovir 400 mg three times daily for 5 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: First-episode genital herpes is treated with oral aciclovir 400 mg TDS for 5 days, started within 5 days of onset or while new lesions are forming. Topical treatment is inadequate for genital disease; suppressive BD dosing is for frequent recurrences; IV aciclovir is reserved for severe/complicated disease.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A patient with genital herpes has 8 troublesome recurrences per year. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Episodic short courses only
No treatment is available for recurrences
A single course of azithromycin
Topical lidocaine alone
Suppressive aciclovir 400 mg twice daily (or valaciclovir 500 mg once daily)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Suppressive aciclovir 400 mg twice daily (or valaciclovir 500 mg once daily)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: Frequent recurrences (≥6 per year) warrant suppressive therapy: aciclovir 400 mg BD (or valaciclovir 500 mg OD), which reduces the frequency and severity of episodes and lowers transmission. Episodic therapy suits less frequent, troublesome recurrences.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A pregnant woman acquires her FIRST episode of genital herpes at 32 weeks' gestation. What is the most appropriate delivery plan and treatment?
options: Vaginal delivery with no antivirals
Elective caesarean, oral aciclovir for the episode, then daily suppressive aciclovir until delivery
Vaginal delivery with suppressive aciclovir from 36 weeks
Immediate induction of labour
Terminate the pregnancy
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Elective caesarean, oral aciclovir for the episode, then daily suppressive aciclovir until delivery
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: A PRIMARY episode in the third trimester (>28 weeks) carries a very high neonatal transmission risk because there is no time to develop and transfer protective antibodies. Elective caesarean is recommended, with aciclovir for the episode and daily suppressive aciclovir 400 mg TDS until delivery.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A woman has a long history of recurrent genital herpes and is now 34 weeks pregnant with no current lesions. What is the correct management regarding delivery?
options: Elective caesarean is mandatory because of her history
Immediate caesarean now
No antivirals and vaginal delivery
Offer suppressive aciclovir 400 mg three times daily from 36 weeks, and plan vaginal delivery
Suppressive aciclovir only if lesions recur
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Offer suppressive aciclovir 400 mg three times daily from 36 weeks, and plan vaginal delivery
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: Recurrent genital herpes carries a low neonatal risk because maternal type-specific antibodies cross the placenta. Suppressive aciclovir 400 mg three times daily from 36 weeks is offered to reduce the chance of lesions at term, and vaginal delivery is planned — a history of recurrences is not an indication for caesarean, and neither are lesions present at the onset of labour.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A woman with a history of recurrent genital herpes presents in labour at term with active vulval ulcers. What is the most appropriate delivery decision?
options: Recommend elective caesarean because active lesions are present
Plan vaginal delivery, explaining that the risk of neonatal herpes with recurrent lesions is low
Delay delivery for 48 hours of aciclovir
Forceps delivery to speed things up
Vaginal delivery with neonatal aciclovir only
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Plan vaginal delivery, explaining that the risk of neonatal herpes with recurrent lesions is low
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: Recurrent genital herpes at term is not an indication for caesarean section, even when lesions are present at the onset of labour: maternal type-specific antibodies cross the placenta and the risk of neonatal herpes is low (0-3%), which does not outweigh the risks of caesarean. Caesarean is recommended instead for a FIRST episode in the third trimester, where transmission risk is much higher. Plan vaginal delivery unless there is another obstetric indication, avoid fetal scalp electrodes, and inform the neonatal team.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A patient newly diagnosed with genital herpes asks whether her partners need to be formally contact-traced. What is the correct advice?
options: Full contact tracing of all partners for 6 months is mandatory
Partners must all take suppressive aciclovir
Contact tracing is not routinely required, but transmission and condom use should be discussed
Her current partner needs a 28-day antiviral course
The infection is notifiable to public health
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Contact tracing is not routinely required, but transmission and condom use should be discussed
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: Unlike bacterial STIs, routine contact tracing/partner notification is not required for genital herpes (as with warts). However, the diagnosis prompts discussion of transmission — including asymptomatic shedding — and condom use, plus a full STI screen and psychological support.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A patient with genital herpes on effective treatment asks whether she can transmit the virus when she has no symptoms. What is the correct advice?
options: She cannot transmit HSV at all unless lesions are visible
Transmission becomes impossible once antibodies have formed
Transmission only ever occurs during the primary episode
Antiviral treatment completely prevents all transmission
Asymptomatic shedding occurs, so transmission is possible even without lesions
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Asymptomatic shedding occurs, so transmission is possible even without lesions
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: HSV undergoes asymptomatic shedding, so transmission can occur even when there are no visible lesions. Condoms reduce but do not eliminate the risk, and suppressive antivirals lower but do not abolish transmission. This is important counselling for patients and partners.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A swab is taken to confirm genital herpes. Which test is the investigation of choice, and how should the sample be taken?
options: Tzanck smear looking for multinucleated giant cells
HSV PCR from the base of a de-roofed vesicle or ulcer
Type-specific HSV serology as the first-line test
Bacterial culture of a swab from intact skin
Serum HSV IgM taken during the acute episode
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: HSV PCR from the base of a de-roofed vesicle or ulcer
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: HSV PCR from a swab of the lesion base is the test of choice — de-roof a vesicle and swab the base, because sampling intact skin gives false negatives. It also types HSV-1 versus HSV-2. Type-specific serology has only a limited role (recurrent ulceration of unknown cause, and primary versus recurrent in pregnancy), and the Tzanck smear is obsolete in UK practice.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A woman acquires primary genital herpes at 20 weeks' gestation. She has no lesions as term approaches. What is the recommended management?
options: Elective caesarean at 39 weeks regardless of lesions
Terminate the pregnancy because of the infection
Give no antivirals at any stage of the pregnancy
Treat the episode, suppressive aciclovir from 36 weeks, and plan vaginal delivery
Deliver by immediate caesarean section at 20 weeks
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Treat the episode, suppressive aciclovir from 36 weeks, and plan vaginal delivery
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: A primary episode BEFORE 28 weeks allows time to develop and transfer protective antibodies, so the neonatal risk at term is lower. Management is to treat the episode, give suppressive aciclovir from 36 weeks, and plan vaginal delivery provided there are no active lesions at term.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A breastfeeding mother with recurrent cold sores (oral HSV) asks about safety of her aciclovir and precautions around the baby. What is the correct advice?
options: Aciclovir is safe in breastfeeding; avoid lesion contact and do not kiss the neonate
She must stop breastfeeding while she is taking aciclovir
Aciclovir is contraindicated during breastfeeding
She should express and discard milk for a week
There are no precautions needed of any kind
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Aciclovir is safe in breastfeeding; avoid lesion contact and do not kiss the neonate
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: Aciclovir/valaciclovir are safe in breastfeeding (minimal transfer), so she can continue. The key precautions are to avoid direct contact between active lesions and the baby and to avoid kissing the neonate while cold sores are active, to prevent neonatal HSV.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: Which statement about the site of HSV latency is correct?
options: Genital HSV lies latent in the trigeminal ganglion
HSV does not become latent
Genital HSV lies latent in the sacral ganglia; oral HSV in the trigeminal ganglion
Both oral and genital HSV lie latent in the dorsal column
Genital HSV lies latent in the brainstem
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Genital HSV lies latent in the sacral ganglia; oral HSV in the trigeminal ganglion
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: After primary infection, HSV establishes latency in sensory nerve ganglia — the sacral ganglia for genital herpes and the trigeminal ganglion for oral cold sores. Reactivation from these ganglia causes recurrent episodes at the corresponding site.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A young man with a first episode of genital herpes has severe pain and has been unable to pass urine for 10 hours. Which complication is this, and how should it be managed?
options: Testicular torsion and infarction
Priapism
Reactive arthritis
Urethral stricture requiring urgent urology referral
Urinary retention — aciclovir and analgesia, urine in a bath, catheterise if he still cannot void
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Urinary retention — aciclovir and analgesia, urine in a bath, catheterise if he still cannot void
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: Severe first-episode genital herpes can cause urinary retention, from painful lesions and occasionally sacral autonomic involvement, and rarely aseptic meningitis. Retention is the commonest reason for admission in a first episode: give oral aciclovir and analgesia, advise passing urine in a bath or under running water, and catheterise (a suprapubic catheter may be more comfortable) if he still cannot void.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: Which of the following best explains why HSV-1 is increasingly a cause of first-episode genital herpes?
options: HSV-1 has become sexually transmitted only recently by mutation
Genital HSV-1 is acquired through oro-genital sex
HSV-1 no longer causes cold sores
HSV-1 is transmitted by blood transfusion
HSV-1 only infects the genitals
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Genital HSV-1 is acquired through oro-genital sex
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: Although HSV-1 classically causes oral cold sores, genital HSV-1 is now a common cause of first-episode genital herpes because it is acquired through oro-genital sex. Genital HSV-1 tends to recur less often than HSV-2.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A patient with an uncomplicated recurrent genital herpes episode that is mild attends the clinic. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Mandatory 6-month suppressive aciclovir
A caesarean section referral
Intravenous aciclovir
Supportive care may suffice, with episodic antiviral courses for troublesome recurrences
Lifelong daily valaciclovir for everyone
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).answer: Supportive care may suffice, with episodic antiviral courses for troublesome recurrences
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: Recurrent episodes are often mild and self-limiting, so supportive care (saline bathing, analgesia) may be enough. Episodic short antiviral courses are used for troublesome recurrences, and suppressive therapy is reserved for frequent recurrences (≥6/year).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).question: A woman is unsure whether a genital herpes episode in early pregnancy is a primary or recurrent infection, which affects her management. Which test helps establish this?
options: HSV type-specific serology (antibody testing)
NAAT of the lesion only
A Tzanck smear
Endocervical culture
A viral load assay
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HSV (genital).explanation: Type-specific HSV serology can help distinguish a primary from a recurrent infection in pregnancy: the presence of type-specific antibodies matching the swabbed virus suggests recurrent (lower-risk) disease, whereas their absence supports a primary (higher-risk) episode. This distinction drives delivery planning.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A 29-year-old man develops fever, sore throat, a maculopapular rash, mouth ulcers and generalised lymphadenopathy about 3 weeks after a high-risk sexual encounter. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV)
Streptococcal pharyngitis
Secondary syphilis
Primary HIV infection (seroconversion illness)
Acute cytomegalovirus infection
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Primary HIV infection (seroconversion illness)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: A glandular-fever-like illness (fever, rash, sore throat, mouth ulcers, lymphadenopathy) 2-4 weeks after a high-risk exposure is classic HIV seroconversion. It is often mistaken for other viral illnesses but the temporal link to exposure is key, and the person is highly infectious. A 4th-generation antibody/p24 test should be done urgently — but at 3 weeks it may still be negative, so discuss with the HIV team, consider an HIV RNA (viral load) test, and repeat the 4th-generation test at 45 days after the exposure.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A newly diagnosed HIV-positive man has a CD4 count of 620 cells/mm³ and feels well. According to BHIVA guidance, when should antiretroviral therapy be started?
options: As soon as possible — ART is offered to everyone regardless of CD4 count
Only when CD4 falls below 350
Only when CD4 falls below 200
Only if he develops an AIDS-defining illness
After a 6-month period of monitoring
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: As soon as possible — ART is offered to everyone regardless of CD4 count
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: Modern guidance is to offer ART to EVERYONE with HIV regardless of CD4 count, starting as soon as possible after diagnosis. Early treatment improves outcomes, allows immune recovery, and achieves U=U. Waiting for a CD4 threshold is outdated.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: Which regimen represents a standard first-line antiretroviral therapy combination?
options: A single NRTI given as monotherapy
An NNRTI given on its own
2 NRTIs plus an integrase inhibitor (e.g. tenofovir + emtricitabine + dolutegravir)
Two protease inhibitors and nothing else
Co-trimoxazole together with aciclovir
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: 2 NRTIs plus an integrase inhibitor (e.g. tenofovir + emtricitabine + dolutegravir)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: Standard first-line ART is 2 NRTIs plus a third agent, now usually an integrase inhibitor — e.g. tenofovir + emtricitabine + dolutegravir. Monotherapy or dual therapy risks resistance; co-trimoxazole is PCP prophylaxis, not ART.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A patient with HIV has a CD4 count of 150 cells/mm³. In addition to ART, which prophylaxis should be started?
options: Aciclovir against herpes
Azithromycin to prevent Mycobacterium avium complex
Fluconazole to prevent cryptococcal meningitis
Isoniazid to prevent tuberculosis
Co-trimoxazole against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Co-trimoxazole against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: When CD4 falls below 200, prophylactic co-trimoxazole is given to prevent Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP). This is stopped once ART restores CD4 above the threshold. Other prophylaxis (e.g. against toxoplasma/MAC) is considered at lower CD4 counts.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A man attends 36 hours after a single episode of receptive anal sex with a male partner who is known to be HIV positive and not on treatment. He is HIV-negative. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start PrEP with daily tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine
Start post-exposure prophylaxis now — 28 days of tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine + raltegravir
Reassure him that no further action is needed
Arrange an HIV test now and review the result before deciding on treatment
Give a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Start post-exposure prophylaxis now — 28 days of tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine + raltegravir
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: He has had a high-risk exposure within 72 hours, so PEP is indicated: tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine + raltegravir (or dolutegravir) for 28 days, started as soon as possible — treatment must not be delayed waiting for a baseline test result. PEP is not recommended beyond 72 hours. PrEP is for ongoing prevention in HIV-negative people, not for a specific recent exposure, though it should be considered after the PEP course if his risk is ongoing.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A HIV-negative man who has sex with men reports ongoing condomless sex with multiple partners and wants to reduce his risk of acquiring HIV. What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Post-exposure prophylaxis after each encounter
HIV vaccination, repeated annually
A single short course of antiretrovirals now
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine, daily or event-based
Long-term co-trimoxazole prophylaxis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine, daily or event-based
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: For an HIV-negative person at ongoing risk, PrEP (tenofovir disoproxil + emtricitabine, daily or event-based 2-1-1 dosing, which is only suitable for anal sex) is highly effective at preventing HIV acquisition. HIV must be excluded before starting, and he then needs HIV and STI testing roughly 3-monthly plus renal monitoring. PrEP does not protect against other STIs. PEP is only for after a specific exposure, and there is no effective HIV vaccine.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A pregnant woman with HIV has a viral load of <50 copies/mL at 36 weeks on ART. What is the most appropriate mode of delivery advice?
options: Vaginal delivery is appropriate
Elective caesarean at 38 weeks
IV zidovudine during a caesarean
Immediate delivery regardless of gestation
Continuous fetal scalp electrode monitoring in labour
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Vaginal delivery is appropriate
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: With a maternal viral load <50 copies/mL at 36 weeks, planned vaginal delivery is appropriate as the risk of vertical transmission is very low. Planned pre-labour caesarean is recommended at 50-399 copies/mL and at 400 or more; IV zidovudine in labour is used if the viral load is unknown or >1000. Invasive fetal monitoring is avoided where the viral load is not suppressed.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: Which AIDS-defining illness is caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) and presents with purple skin/mucosal lesions?
options: Cytomegalovirus retinitis
Pneumocystis pneumonia
Kaposi's sarcoma
CNS lymphoma
Cryptococcal meningitis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Kaposi's sarcoma
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and presents as purple/violaceous papules and plaques on the skin and mucosa (and can involve GI/respiratory tracts). It is managed with ART plus radiotherapy/resection ± systemic therapy. CNS lymphoma is EBV-related.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A patient with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 40 cells/mm³ develops visual disturbance and is found to have retinitis. Which opportunistic infection is most likely?
options: Toxoplasma retinitis
Pneumocystis choroiditis
Herpes simplex keratitis
Candida endophthalmitis
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: CMV retinitis (and colitis) characteristically occurs at very low CD4 counts (<50) and causes visual disturbance or loss. It is a sight-threatening AIDS-defining condition requiring urgent ophthalmology and HIV specialist referral alongside ART.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A patient on effective ART has had a sustained undetectable viral load for over a year. His partner asks about the risk of sexual transmission. What is the correct advice?
options: He remains highly infectious despite treatment
Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U): he cannot transmit HIV sexually while the viral load remains undetectable
Transmission risk is halved but still significant
He can only transmit during seroconversion
Condoms make no difference so are unnecessary for any reason
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U): he cannot transmit HIV sexually while the viral load remains undetectable
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: U=U is a foundational principle: a person on effective ART with a sustained undetectable viral load cannot transmit HIV sexually. (Condoms may still be advised for other STI prevention/contraception, but the HIV transmission risk via sex is effectively zero while undetectable.)

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A 25-year-old HIV-positive woman asks about cancer screening. Which additional screening is specifically recommended because of her HIV?
options: Six-monthly mammography from age 25
Three-monthly CA-125
Annual colonoscopy
Annual cervical smears due to increased HPV/cervical cancer risk
No additional screening is needed
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Annual cervical smears due to increased HPV/cervical cancer risk
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: Women with HIV are at increased risk of HPV-related cervical disease, so annual cervical smears are recommended (more frequent than the general population). Other holistic care includes vaccinations, cardiovascular risk management and bone/renal monitoring.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A baby is born to an HIV-positive mother whose viral load was <50 copies/mL throughout. What neonatal prophylaxis is most appropriate?
options: Zidovudine monotherapy for 2–4 weeks
No prophylaxis is needed for this baby
Combination zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine for 4 weeks
Co-trimoxazole given from birth onwards
A single dose of nevirapine and nothing more
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Zidovudine monotherapy for 2–4 weeks
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: Neonatal post-exposure prophylaxis should be started as soon as possible after birth. For a low-risk infant (maternal viral load <50), it is zidovudine alone for 2-4 weeks; high-risk infants receive combination prophylaxis (zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine) for 4 weeks.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: Which statement about HIV diagnostic testing is correct?
options: Viral load is the initial screening test of choice
HIV can be reliably excluded 3 days after exposure
A 4th-generation test is negative-conclusive only at 45 days after exposure
The CD4 count is what is used to diagnose HIV
Only a lymph node biopsy can confirm the diagnosis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: A 4th-generation test is negative-conclusive only at 45 days after exposure
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: The standard diagnostic is a 4th-generation lab test detecting HIV antibody plus p24 antigen. Most infections are detected by about 4 weeks, but the window period is 45 days: only a negative test at or after 45 days from the last exposure reliably excludes HIV, so an earlier negative must be repeated. A reactive result needs a confirmatory assay. CD4 count and viral load are used for staging and monitoring, not diagnosis.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A HIV-positive man with a CD4 of 180 develops a dry cough and marked breathlessness on exertion with desaturation on walking, and a clear-ish chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Bacterial lobar pneumonia
Tuberculosis
Pulmonary Kaposi's sarcoma
Pulmonary embolism
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: A subacute dry cough with exertional breathlessness and desaturation at a CD4 <200, often with a relatively unremarkable early chest X-ray, is classic for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Treatment (and prophylaxis) is with co-trimoxazole; steroids are added if hypoxic.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a patient known to be HIV-positive. How soon should post-exposure prophylaxis ideally be started?
options: Within 2 weeks
As soon as possible and within 72 hours
Only after confirmatory HIV testing at 6 weeks
Within 7 days
There is no time limit
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: As soon as possible and within 72 hours
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: Occupational PEP should be started as soon as possible and within 72 hours of exposure (the sooner the better); it is not recommended beyond 72 hours. The regimen is tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine + raltegravir (or dolutegravir) for 28 days, with a baseline HIV test and a repeat 4th-generation test 45 days after completing the course.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A patient prefers not to take daily HIV tablets. Which modern ART option could be offered?
options: Co-trimoxazole monotherapy
PrEP instead of ART
A single annual infusion of tenofovir
Long-acting injectable ART given every 2 months
Stopping treatment intermittently
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Long-acting injectable ART given every 2 months
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: Long-acting injectable ART, given every 2 months, is an option for people who prefer not to take daily oral therapy, provided they are suitable and already virologically suppressed. PrEP is for HIV-negative people, not treatment.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: Which of the following best distinguishes PrEP from PEP?
options: PrEP is taken by HIV-negative people to prevent acquisition; PEP is a 28-day course after an exposure
PrEP is taken after an exposure; PEP is taken beforehand
They are identical regimens with two different names
PrEP is for HIV-positive people; PEP is for HIV-negative people
PEP is a lifelong daily tablet taken indefinitely
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: PrEP is taken by HIV-negative people to prevent acquisition; PEP is a 28-day course after an exposure
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: PrEP (tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine, daily or event-based) is taken by HIV-negative people at ongoing risk to prevent acquisition. PEP is started AFTER a specific potential exposure, within 72 hours, as a 28-day course (tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine + raltegravir) to prevent seroconversion.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A pregnant woman with HIV presents in labour and her most recent viral load is >1000 copies/mL. In addition to planning delivery, what intrapartum intervention is indicated?
options: Oral co-trimoxazole
Immediate breastfeeding to boost infant immunity
IV zidovudine during labour/delivery
Stopping all ART during labour
A single dose of nevirapine to the mother only
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: IV zidovudine during labour/delivery
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: With a high (>1000 copies/mL) or unknown viral load, IV zidovudine is given during labour and delivery to reduce vertical transmission. Because she is already in labour a pre-labour caesarean is no longer possible — the obstetric team decides between urgent caesarean and expediting vaginal delivery. The neonate is then treated as high-risk and receives combination post-exposure prophylaxis.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: An HIV-positive mother who is fully suppressed on ART wishes to breastfeed. What is the correct UK advice?
options: Breastfeeding is absolutely forbidden in all circumstances
Mixed feeding is the safest option for the infant
She should breastfeed freely, as it carries no risk at all
She must stop her ART for the duration of breastfeeding
Formula feeding is recommended, but a fully suppressed mother who chooses to breastfeed is supported
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Formula feeding is recommended, but a fully suppressed mother who chooses to breastfeed is supported
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: Formula feeding is recommended because it carries no risk of postnatal transmission. However, a woman who is fully virologically suppressed on ART and adherent and who chooses to breastfeed should be supported, not refused — with counselling that the risk is low but not zero, that feeding should be exclusive, and with monthly maternal viral load and infant testing during breastfeeding and for 2 months after stopping. Mixed feeding is discouraged.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: Which infection can occur at any CD4 count and is the commonest HIV-associated opportunistic infection globally?
options: Cytomegalovirus
Tuberculosis
Cryptococcal meningitis
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
Cerebral toxoplasmosis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Tuberculosis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: Tuberculosis can occur at any CD4 count and is the commonest HIV-associated opportunistic infection worldwide. Others such as CMV (CD4 <50), PCP (CD4 <200) and cryptococcal meningitis tend to occur at lower CD4 counts.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A patient's HIV viral load is reported as 'undetectable (<50 copies/mL)' after starting ART. What does this indicate?
options: The virus has been eradicated and ART can stop
The patient never had HIV
The test has failed
Effective viral suppression — the treatment goal — but ART must continue lifelong
Immediate immunity to reinfection
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Effective viral suppression — the treatment goal — but ART must continue lifelong
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: An undetectable viral load (<50 copies/mL) indicates effective suppression — the goal of ART — leading to immune recovery and U=U. However, HIV is not eradicated (it persists in reservoirs), so ART must be continued lifelong; stopping would allow viral rebound.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.question: A patient with advanced HIV develops progressive focal neurological signs and a ring-enhancing brain lesion on imaging. Which AIDS-associated condition is the most likely cause?
options: Cerebral toxoplasmosis
Bacterial brain abscess
Migraine
Multiple sclerosis
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.answer: Cerebral toxoplasmosis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__HIV (clinical.explanation: In advanced HIV, cerebral toxoplasmosis classically causes focal neurological deficits with ring-enhancing lesions on brain imaging. Primary CNS lymphoma (EBV-related) is the main differential; empirical anti-toxoplasma treatment with follow-up imaging is often used to distinguish them.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A 26-year-old man presents with dysuria and a profuse, purulent green urethral discharge. A urethral Gram stain shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci. What is the most likely diagnosis and the correct first-line treatment when sensitivities are not yet known?
options: Chlamydia — doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days
Non-gonococcal urethritis — ofloxacin
Gonorrhoea — azithromycin 1 g single dose
Gonorrhoea — ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose (monotherapy)
Gonorrhoea — ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO empirically
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: Gonorrhoea — ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose (monotherapy)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci with purulent discharge indicate gonorrhoea. When sensitivities are unknown, first-line is ceftriaxone 1 g IM monotherapy. Azithromycin has been dropped (rising resistance), and ciprofloxacin is reserved for people who cannot have ceftriaxone, and only when culture confirms a sensitive isolate.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: When managing gonorrhoea, which investigation is essential BEFORE giving treatment and distinguishes its work-up from chlamydia?
options: A charcoal swab for culture and sensitivities
A test of cure by NAAT
Serum antibody testing
A cervical smear
A blood culture
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: A charcoal swab for culture and sensitivities
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Because of high and rising gonococcal resistance, a charcoal swab for culture and sensitivities must be taken before treatment (NAAT confirms the organism but only culture gives sensitivities). This pre-treatment culture step is a key difference from chlamydia management.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A woman is treated with ceftriaxone 1 g IM for gonorrhoea diagnosed on NAAT; no culture result is available. Regarding a test of cure, what is the correct advice?
options: A test of cure is not needed as ceftriaxone is highly effective
A test of cure is only needed if she becomes pregnant
Yes — her susceptibility is unknown, so NAAT at least 2 weeks after treatment
Repeat the NAAT at 24 hours to confirm cure
A test of cure is only ever needed for men
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: Yes — her susceptibility is unknown, so NAAT at least 2 weeks after treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Test of cure is recommended when susceptibility is unknown, as here, and also for pharyngeal infection, persistent symptoms, treatment with anything other than ceftriaxone, and pregnancy. It is done by NAAT at least 2 weeks after treatment, since earlier testing detects dead organisms; culture at least 72 hours after treatment is used if symptoms persist. Routine TOC is only unnecessary for uncomplicated anogenital infection treated with ceftriaxone where culture confirms susceptibility.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: Which statement about the tissue tropism of Neisseria gonorrhoeae is correct?
options: It preferentially infects squamous vaginal epithelium
It preferentially infects keratinised skin surfaces
It can only ever infect the urethra
It cannot infect the pharynx or the rectum at all
It infects mucous membranes lined by columnar epithelium, not squamous vagina
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: It infects mucous membranes lined by columnar epithelium, not squamous vagina
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Gonorrhoea infects columnar epithelium — endocervix, urethra, rectum, conjunctiva and pharynx — but not the squamous vaginal epithelium. This tropism explains why endocervical/urethral/rectal/pharyngeal sites are affected and why testing at all sites of exposure matters.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A neonate develops a profuse purulent conjunctivitis with marked lid swelling within the first 48 hours of life, born vaginally to an untreated mother. What is the most concerning diagnosis and why is it urgent?
options: Chlamydial conjunctivitis — mild and entirely self-limiting
Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum — can cause corneal perforation and blindness
Chemical conjunctivitis — needs no specific treatment
Viral conjunctivitis — supportive care only
Allergic conjunctivitis — treat with topical antihistamine
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum — can cause corneal perforation and blindness
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Early (first few days), profuse, purulent neonatal conjunctivitis suggests gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum — a medical emergency that can cause corneal perforation and blindness and is associated with sepsis, needing same-day review and a systemic third-generation cephalosporin. Chlamydial ophthalmia usually presents later (around 5-14 days) and is less aggressive, but it is not self-limiting: it needs systemic oral antibiotic treatment because of the risk of chlamydial pneumonitis.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A young woman presents with fever, painful migratory joint pains, tenosynovitis of the wrists, and scattered pustular skin lesions. She recently had unprotected sex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis
Gout
Reactive arthritis from chlamydia
Disseminated gonococcal infection
Systemic lupus erythematosus
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: The triad of dermatitis (pustular/haemorrhagic lesions), migratory polyarthritis/arthralgia and tenosynovitis in a sexually active young person is classic for disseminated gonococcal infection, from haematogenous spread. It may progress to purulent septic arthritis and, rarely, endocarditis or meningitis. DGI needs daily parenteral ceftriaxone for at least a week — not the single-dose regimen used for uncomplicated infection — with cultures from blood, joint and all mucosal sites.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A patient with a documented severe cephalosporin allergy is diagnosed with gonorrhoea, and culture confirms the isolate is ciprofloxacin-sensitive. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose — appropriate here because ceftriaxone cannot be used and the isolate is confirmed sensitive
Ciprofloxacin should be used routinely whenever the isolate is sensitive, to avoid the injection
Azithromycin 1 g single dose is preferred
No antibiotic is needed
Doxycycline for 7 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose — appropriate here because ceftriaxone cannot be used and the isolate is confirmed sensitive
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM remains first line for everyone, including people whose isolate is ciprofloxacin-sensitive. Ciprofloxacin is reserved for those who cannot have ceftriaxone, and only when culture confirms sensitivity, because quinolones should be used only when other antibiotics are inappropriate (MHRA).

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: Why has azithromycin been dropped from the standard empirical gonorrhoea regimen?
options: It caused an unacceptable number of allergic reactions
It is no longer manufactured in the UK
Rising azithromycin resistance — ceftriaxone monotherapy covers reduced-susceptibility strains
It is ineffective against coexisting chlamydia infection
It interacts dangerously with ceftriaxone when co-administered
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: Rising azithromycin resistance — ceftriaxone monotherapy covers reduced-susceptibility strains
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: The dual regimen (ceftriaxone + azithromycin) was replaced by ceftriaxone 1 g IM monotherapy because of rising azithromycin resistance. The higher ceftriaxone dose covers strains with reduced cephalosporin susceptibility, and removing azithromycin reduces selection pressure for resistance.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A man diagnosed with gonorrhoea is also found to have chlamydia on his STI screen. How should this be managed?
options: Treat only the gonorrhoea, as it is more serious
No treatment until sensitivities for both return
A single dose of azithromycin will cover both
Treat only the chlamydia and recheck later
Treat the gonorrhoea with ceftriaxone AND the chlamydia with doxycycline
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: Treat the gonorrhoea with ceftriaxone AND the chlamydia with doxycycline
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Chlamydia coinfection is common, so both are treated — gonorrhoea specifically with ceftriaxone 1 g IM and chlamydia with doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days. In pregnancy doxycycline is contraindicated, so coexisting chlamydia is treated with azithromycin instead, and a test of cure is recommended. A full STI screen and GUM referral for partner notification are also standard.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: Which feature most reliably distinguishes typical gonorrhoea from typical chlamydia at presentation?
options: Gonorrhoea is usually asymptomatic; chlamydia is usually symptomatic
Gonorrhoea is more often symptomatic with a purulent green/yellow discharge; chlamydia is largely asymptomatic
Both are always symptomatic
Chlamydia causes purulent green discharge; gonorrhoea causes none
Only chlamydia causes dysuria
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: Gonorrhoea is more often symptomatic with a purulent green/yellow discharge; chlamydia is largely asymptomatic
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Gonorrhoea is more often symptomatic and classically produces a purulent green/yellow discharge with dysuria, whereas chlamydia is largely asymptomatic and often detected on screening. Note the limits of this rule: roughly half of women with urogenital gonorrhoea, and most pharyngeal and rectal infections, are asymptomatic.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A GUM clinic wants to detect gonorrhoea at all potential sites in an MSM patient who reports oral and anal sex. Which testing approach is correct?
options: A first-catch urine sample on its own
An endocervical swab on its own
A single blood test for gonococcal antibodies
NAAT at urethra/urine plus rectal and pharyngeal swabs, with culture before treatment
A pharyngeal swab on its own
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: NAAT at urethra/urine plus rectal and pharyngeal swabs, with culture before treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Because gonorrhoea infects columnar epithelium at multiple sites (often silently in the pharynx and rectum), NAAT should be performed at all sites of exposure — urethral/urine plus rectal and pharyngeal swabs — with charcoal culture swabs taken for sensitivities. Testing only one site would miss extragenital infection.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A patient treated for pharyngeal gonorrhoea returns for follow-up. Why is a test of cure particularly important for this site?
options: It is harder to eradicate and often asymptomatic, so TOC is especially important
Pharyngeal infection is always symptomatic so cure is obvious
The pharynx cannot reliably be re-tested afterwards
A test of cure is never needed for pharyngeal infection
A test of cure is only ever done for genital sites
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: It is harder to eradicate and often asymptomatic, so TOC is especially important
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Pharyngeal gonorrhoea is more difficult to eradicate and is often asymptomatic, and with rising resistance a test of cure is specifically recommended after pharyngeal infection to confirm eradication.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A 30-year-old woman with gonococcal cervicitis develops lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness and fever. What complication has developed and what is the long-term risk?
options: Bartholin's cyst — no long-term risk
Ovarian torsion — risk of loss of ovary
Pelvic inflammatory disease — risk of infertility and ectopic pregnancy
Endometriosis — risk of dysmenorrhoea
Urethral stricture — risk of retention
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: Pelvic inflammatory disease — risk of infertility and ectopic pregnancy
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Ascending gonococcal infection causes pelvic inflammatory disease (lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, fever), which risks tubal damage leading to infertility and ectopic pregnancy. This requires prompt broad empirical PID treatment.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A symptomatic man's urethral Gram stain shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci. What does this allow, and what must still be done?
options: A definitive cure without the need for antibiotics
That azithromycin monotherapy will now be sufficient
Immediate discharge with no treatment required
Confirmation that there is no coexisting chlamydia
A rapid presumptive diagnosis — but still take a culture swab before treating
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: A rapid presumptive diagnosis — but still take a culture swab before treating
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: A urethral Gram stain showing gram-negative intracellular diplococci gives a rapid presumptive diagnosis in symptomatic men, allowing prompt ceftriaxone treatment. A charcoal swab for culture and sensitivities should still be taken beforehand because of resistance, and chlamydia coinfection should be tested for and treated.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: Which of the following best explains why antimicrobial stewardship is emphasised so heavily in gonorrhoea?
options: Gonorrhoea is now effectively untreatable in the UK
Ceftriaxone is the last reliable first-line agent, and resistant strains are emerging
Antibiotics have no useful effect on gonorrhoea at all
Antimicrobial resistance only affects chlamydia
Gonorrhoea always resolves without any treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: Ceftriaxone is the last reliable first-line agent, and resistant strains are emerging
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Gonococci have sequentially developed resistance to penicillins, tetracyclines and quinolones, leaving ceftriaxone as the last reliable first-line agent — and resistant strains are already emerging. This drives the stewardship measures: higher-dose monotherapy, mandatory culture with sensitivities, and test of cure for all cases.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A 22-year-old woman is diagnosed with gonorrhoea and asks when she can resume sexual activity. What is the correct advice?
options: Immediately after the ceftriaxone injection
After her next menstrual period has finished
After 24 hours have passed since the injection
No sex, including oral sex, until 7 days after she and her partners finish treatment
There are no restrictions once her symptoms improve
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: No sex, including oral sex, until 7 days after she and her partners finish treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: Advise no sex, including oral sex, until 7 days after the patient and all partners have completed treatment and symptoms have settled, to prevent reinfection and onward transmission. This is separate from the test of cure, which is done later. GUM referral for partner notification and testing for other STIs are also part of management.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: A patient with a severe cephalosporin allergy is diagnosed with gonorrhoea, and sensitivities are not yet available. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Seek specialist GUM advice for an alternative guided by culture sensitivities
Give the ceftriaxone anyway and observe her closely
Give azithromycin 1 g alone as monotherapy instead
Withhold all treatment until the patient can tolerate ceftriaxone
Treat with a 7-day course of doxycycline alone
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.answer: Seek specialist GUM advice for an alternative guided by culture sensitivities
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: With a genuine severe cephalosporin allergy, first-line ceftriaxone cannot be given, so specialist GUM advice is needed and treatment is guided by culture and sensitivities — for example ciprofloxacin if the isolate is confirmed sensitive, or second-line options such as gentamicin with azithromycin. All of these require a test of cure. Azithromycin or doxycycline monotherapy is inadequate for gonorrhoea given resistance.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.question: Which of the following is a recognised local complication of gonorrhoea in men?
options: Reactive arthritis only
Testicular torsion
Epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis and urethral strictures
Varicocele
Hydronephrosis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Gonorrhoea.explanation: In men, gonorrhoea can cause epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis and urethral strictures. In women it can cause PID leading to infertility and ectopic pregnancy. Disseminated infection and increased HIV transmission are additional important complications.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A 17-year-old boy presents with sudden, severe left testicular pain for 2 hours with vomiting. The testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie and the cremasteric reflex is absent. There are no urinary symptoms. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Empirical ceftriaxone and doxycycline for epididymo-orchitis
Ofloxacin and scrotal support
Urgent scrotal Doppler ultrasound before any intervention
Urgent surgical scrotal exploration
Reassurance and analgesia with GP follow-up
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: This is testicular torsion (sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex, young age). Torsion is a surgical emergency with a ~6-hour salvage window, so the correct action is urgent surgical exploration — NOT waiting for an ultrasound. Imaging must not delay exploration when torsion is clinically suspected.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A 24-year-old sexually active man has a 2-day history of gradually worsening right scrotal pain and swelling, with urethral discharge and dysuria. The cremasteric reflex is present. Torsion is felt to be excluded. What is the most likely causative organism group?
options: Sexually transmitted organisms — Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Enteric organisms such as E. coli from a urinary source
Mycobacterium tuberculosis seeding the epididymis
Mumps virus following a subclinical parotitis
Candida albicans from a genital yeast infection
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: Sexually transmitted organisms — Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: In a younger (<35), sexually active man with urethral discharge, the likely cause is sexually transmitted — chlamydia and gonorrhoea. Enteric organisms (E. coli) predominate in older, low-risk men with urinary symptoms or instrumentation. The gradual onset, present cremasteric reflex and urethral symptoms fit epididymo-orchitis rather than torsion.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A 24-year-old man with suspected STI-related epididymo-orchitis needs empirical treatment before culture results. According to current BASHH guidance, what is the correct regimen?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM + doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days
Ofloxacin 200 mg BD for 14 days
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose + doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 10–14 days
Azithromycin 1 g single dose only
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for 7 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose + doxycycline 100 mg PO BD for 10–14 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: For a likely STI cause, treat with ceftriaxone 1 g IM (single dose) plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 10-14 days. The dose is 1 g, not the older 500 mg (BASHH). Ofloxacin alone would be for an enteric cause.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A 68-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia and a recent urinary catheter develops gradual-onset right scrotal pain with dysuria and positive nitrites on dipstick. Torsion is excluded. What is the most appropriate empirical treatment?
options: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM + doxycycline for 14 days
No antibiotics — analgesia alone
Azithromycin 1 g single dose
Benzathine penicillin
Ofloxacin 200 mg PO BD for 14 days (covering enteric organisms)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: Ofloxacin 200 mg PO BD for 14 days (covering enteric organisms)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: In an older, low-sexual-risk man with urinary symptoms and recent instrumentation, the cause is enteric (E. coli), so a quinolone is used because it penetrates the testis well — ofloxacin 200 mg BD for 14 days, or levofloxacin 500 mg OD for 10 days. Fluoroquinolones may only be prescribed when other antibiotics are inappropriate (MHRA), and the patient must be counselled about tendon rupture, aortic aneurysm/dissection and neuropathy. STI-directed ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is for sexually acquired disease.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: Which examination finding is most reassuring AGAINST testicular torsion but must never be used alone to exclude it?
options: A high-riding testis
A present cremasteric reflex
Absent bowel sounds
A horizontal testicular lie
Nausea and vomiting
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: A present cremasteric reflex favours epididymo-orchitis over torsion (in which it is typically absent). However, no single sign — including Prehn's sign or the cremasteric reflex — is reliable enough to exclude torsion; if torsion cannot be confidently excluded, urgent surgical exploration is required.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A man treated empirically for STI-related epididymo-orchitis asks what else is required beyond his antibiotics. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: No further action is needed once the antibiotics have been prescribed
Lifelong prophylactic antibiotics to prevent recurrent episodes
A test of cure at 48 hours to confirm the infection has cleared
No sex until treatment is complete, plus GUM referral for a full STI screen and partner notification
Immediate orchidectomy to prevent spread of the infection
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: No sex until treatment is complete, plus GUM referral for a full STI screen and partner notification
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: When the cause is an STI, management includes advising no sex until treatment is complete and referral to GUM for a full STI screen and partner notification, in addition to the antibiotics and supportive measures. This prevents onward transmission and reinfection.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A 30-year-old man reports insertive anal sex and now has epididymo-orchitis. Given a mixed STI and enteric risk, what is the most appropriate empirical treatment?
options: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM + ofloxacin 200 mg BD for 14 days
Doxycycline alone for 14 days
Ofloxacin alone for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose only
Azithromycin 1 g single dose
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM + ofloxacin 200 mg BD for 14 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: With mixed STI and enteric risk (e.g. insertive anal sex), cover both by combining ceftriaxone 1 g IM (for gonorrhoea) with ofloxacin 200 mg BD for 14 days (for chlamydia and enteric organisms). Single-agent therapy would leave one likely pathogen group untreated.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A scrotal Doppler ultrasound is being considered in a young man with acute scrotal pain in whom torsion cannot be clinically excluded. What is the correct approach?
options: Perform the ultrasound first and act on the result
Discharge with oral antibiotics and outpatient scan
Proceed to urgent surgical exploration without delaying for imaging
Repeat clinical examination in 24 hours
Give analgesia and reassess in the morning
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: Proceed to urgent surgical exploration without delaying for imaging
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: If torsion cannot be excluded clinically, urgent surgical exploration is mandatory and must NOT be delayed for imaging — salvage rates fall sharply beyond about 6 hours. Doppler ultrasound can support a diagnosis of epididymo-orchitis, but normal or preserved flow does NOT exclude torsion, so a negative scan must never overturn a clinical suspicion that warrants exploration.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A 22-year-old man is found on urethral Gram stain to have gram-negative intracellular diplococci alongside his epididymo-orchitis. Which organism does this indicate and how does it affect treatment?
options: Chlamydia — treat with doxycycline alone
Mumps virus — supportive care only
E. coli — treat with ofloxacin alone
Mycobacterium tuberculosis — start anti-TB therapy
Neisseria gonorrhoeae — ensure ceftriaxone is included
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: Neisseria gonorrhoeae — ensure ceftriaxone is included
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci indicate Neisseria gonorrhoeae, so treatment must include ceftriaxone 1 g IM (plus doxycycline to cover co-existing chlamydia). This is why the STI regimen is dual therapy rather than doxycycline alone.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A previously well 19-year-old presents with bilateral testicular pain and swelling a few days after parotid gland swelling and fever. What is the most likely cause of his orchitis?
options: Chlamydia trachomatis
Mumps orchitis (a non-STI viral cause)
E. coli
Testicular torsion
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: Orchitis following parotitis and fever is classic mumps orchitis — a non-STI viral cause appearing about 4–8 days after the parotid swelling. It is usually UNILATERAL, with bilateral involvement in a minority, and bilateral disease is what threatens fertility. Management is supportive; mumps is vaccine-preventable (MMR) and is a notifiable disease. It must be distinguished from bacterial epididymo-orchitis and from torsion.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A 40-year-old man has a persistent, painless testicular mass that does not settle after treatment for presumed epididymo-orchitis. What is the key red-flag diagnosis to exclude?
options: Inguinal hernia
Varicocele
Hydrocele
Testicular tumour
Chronic epididymitis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: A persistent, painless testicular mass is a red flag for testicular tumour, which must be excluded (ultrasound + tumour markers). Epididymo-orchitis that fails to settle should prompt re-imaging to look for an abscess or an underlying tumour.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: Which of the following best distinguishes the typical ONSET of epididymo-orchitis from testicular torsion?
options: Epididymo-orchitis develops more gradually over hours to days; torsion is sudden and severe
Epididymo-orchitis is sudden and severe; torsion is gradual
Both have an identical instantaneous onset
Torsion always develops over several days
Onset is never helpful in distinguishing them
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: Epididymo-orchitis develops more gradually over hours to days; torsion is sudden and severe
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: Epididymo-orchitis typically develops more gradually over hours to days, often with urinary/urethral symptoms and fever, whereas torsion is characteristically sudden and severe (often <6 hours) with vomiting. Onset helps but does not replace the need to exclude torsion in any acute scrotum.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A man with STI-related epididymo-orchitis is being treated. Which complication is most associated with bilateral disease?
options: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
Inguinal hernia
Reduced fertility
Reactive arthritis
Hydronephrosis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: Reduced fertility is a recognised complication, particularly with bilateral epididymo-orchitis (as also seen with bilateral mumps orchitis). Other complications include abscess formation, testicular infarction/atrophy, hydrocele/pyocele and chronic scrotal pain.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A 26-year-old man with epididymo-orchitis is treated with ofloxacin because of a possible enteric cause. What important prescribing caution applies to this drug class?
options: They may be prescribed freely for any genital infection, as no class-wide restrictions now apply
They are the first-line antibiotic for every cause of epididymo-orchitis, whatever the organism
They must be stopped only if the patient develops a mild rash, and are otherwise safe long term
They should be avoided in anyone taking paracetamol because of a dangerous drug interaction
They may only be used when other antibiotics are inappropriate, with counselling about tendon rupture (MHRA)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: They may only be used when other antibiotics are inappropriate, with counselling about tendon rupture (MHRA)
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: Since the MHRA restriction, systemic fluoroquinolones (ofloxacin, levofloxacin) may only be prescribed when other antibiotics are inappropriate — because of disabling and potentially irreversible reactions including tendinitis and tendon rupture, aortic aneurysm and dissection, peripheral neuropathy and CNS effects. They are still used for the enteric cause of epididymo-orchitis because of their testicular penetration, but the patient must be counselled and told to stop the drug at the first sign of tendon pain.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A young man presents with an acute scrotum. Which single principle should govern the initial approach regardless of the eventual diagnosis?
options: Start antibiotics immediately and arrange review in a week
Exclude testicular torsion first, proceeding to urgent exploration if it cannot be excluded clinically
Arrange an outpatient ultrasound and provide analgesia meanwhile
Reassure the patient, as most acute scrotal pain is benign
Perform a full STI screen before anything else is considered
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: Exclude testicular torsion first, proceeding to urgent exploration if it cannot be excluded clinically
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: In any acute scrotum, testicular torsion must be excluded first because it is a time-critical surgical emergency (salvage <6 hours). If torsion cannot be excluded clinically, proceed to urgent surgical exploration without delaying for imaging — only once torsion is excluded do you work up and treat epididymo-orchitis by likely organism.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.question: A 33-year-old man with epididymo-orchitis of uncertain cause is started on treatment but his symptoms are not settling after several days. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue the same treatment for 3 months
Stop all antibiotics and observe
Immediately perform orchidectomy
Re-image the scrotum to look for an abscess or underlying tumour
Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.answer: Re-image the scrotum to look for an abscess or underlying tumour
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Epididymo-orc.explanation: Failure to settle warrants re-imaging (scrotal ultrasound) to look for complications such as an abscess or an underlying testicular tumour, and to reconsider the diagnosis/organism. Follow-up is an explicit part of management; premature surgery or simply continuing ineffective treatment is inappropriate.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A 21-year-old sexually active woman attends for a routine check and has no symptoms. According to the National Chlamydia Screening Programme, what is the most appropriate action?
options: No screening is needed as she is asymptomatic
Perform an endocervical swab under direct vision only
Screen only if she requests it
Offer chlamydia screening (annually or on change of partner) with a self-taken vulvovaginal swab
Screen for chlamydia with a blood test
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: Offer chlamydia screening (annually or on change of partner) with a self-taken vulvovaginal swab
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: Opportunistic screening is offered to women and people with a cervix aged 15-24, annually or on change of partner, precisely because most infections are asymptomatic — this 21-year-old is in that group. In women the first-line NAAT specimen is a vulvovaginal swab, which can be self-taken. Chlamydia is diagnosed by NAAT, not serology.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A 23-year-old man has urethral discomfort and a positive first-catch urine NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis. He has no allergies and is not on other medication. What is the first-line treatment?
options: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
Azithromycin 1 g single dose
Ceftriaxone 1 g intramuscular single dose
Erythromycin 500 mg four times daily for 7 days
Benzathine penicillin single dose
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: First-line for uncomplicated chlamydia is doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days. Single-dose azithromycin has been removed as a routine option because doxycycline has higher cure rates (especially rectal infection and against Mycoplasma genitalium). Ceftriaxone is for gonorrhoea; penicillin is for syphilis.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A pregnant woman at 12 weeks tests positive for uncomplicated genital chlamydia. What is the most appropriate treatment and follow-up?
options: Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days, no test of cure
A single dose of ciprofloxacin
Azithromycin 1 g then 500 mg OD for 2 days (or erythromycin), with a test of cure
No treatment at all until after delivery
Doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days instead
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: Azithromycin 1 g then 500 mg OD for 2 days (or erythromycin), with a test of cure
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy, so the regimen is azithromycin 1 g stat then 500 mg OD for 2 days (or erythromycin 500 mg QDS for 7 days, or amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 7 days). A test of cure IS recommended in pregnancy, done at least 3 weeks after finishing treatment. Untreated chlamydia risks preterm birth, PROM and neonatal conjunctivitis/pneumonia.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A 20-year-old woman treated for chlamydia asks when she can have sex again. What is the correct advice?
options: Immediately after taking the antibiotics
After 24 hours
After her next period
After a negative test of cure at 1 week
After 7 days and once all partners have completed treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: After 7 days and once all partners have completed treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: Advise no sex until the 7-day course is completed AND until all partners have completed treatment, to avoid reinfection. Referral to GUM for contact tracing (6 months or to the last partner, but 4 weeks before symptom onset for a man with symptomatic urethritis) and testing for other STIs are also part of management.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: An MSM patient presents with a change in bowel habit, anal pain, tenesmus and rectal discharge, and is found to have a rectal chlamydia NAAT positive for an L-serovar. What is the diagnosis and the correct treatment?
options: Uncomplicated chlamydia — doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days
Lymphogranuloma venereum — doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days
Gonococcal proctitis — ceftriaxone single dose
Inflammatory bowel disease — mesalazine
Herpes proctitis — aciclovir
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: Lymphogranuloma venereum — doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: Serovars L1–L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum, which in MSM classically presents with proctocolitis (can mimic IBD). LGV requires a longer course: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days (vs 7 days for uncomplicated chlamydia). HIV co-infection is common and should be tested for.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A woman is treated for chlamydia. Regarding a repeat NAAT test, which statement is correct?
options: A test of cure is routinely required for all patients at 1 week
NAAT should be repeated at 48 hours to confirm eradication
A repeat test at 3 months counts as a test of cure
Not routine, but done in pregnancy, rectal infection or poor adherence — at least 3 weeks after
No repeat testing of any kind is ever needed after treatment
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: Not routine, but done in pregnancy, rectal infection or poor adherence — at least 3 weeks after
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: A test of cure is not routine (treatment is highly effective) but is recommended in pregnancy, for rectal infection, if symptoms persist, or if adherence was poor or re-exposure is likely — and must be delayed to at least 3 weeks after treatment finishes, because a NAAT can remain positive for 3-5 weeks from dead organisms. The separate 3-month re-test detects reinfection, not cure.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A 19-year-old man develops bilateral conjunctivitis, dysuria and an acutely swollen painful knee two weeks after an episode of urethritis. What is the most likely underlying trigger?
options: Chlamydia-triggered reactive arthritis
Gonococcal septic arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis
Gout
Syphilitic arthropathy
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: The triad of conjunctivitis, urethritis and arthritis ('can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree') is reactive arthritis, classically triggered by chlamydia. It is a sterile, post-infectious arthritis rather than direct joint infection, so the joint fluid is not purulent with organisms.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: Which is the correct first-line NAAT specimen for detecting genital chlamydia in a woman and in a man respectively?
options: Endocervical swab in women; urethral swab in men
First-catch urine in women; vulvovaginal swab in men
Vulvovaginal swab in women; first-catch urine in men
Blood serology in both
High vaginal swab in women; mid-stream urine in men
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: Vulvovaginal swab in women; first-catch urine in men
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: NAAT is the diagnostic test. The first-line specimens are a vulvovaginal swab in women (self-taken is acceptable and as sensitive) and a first-catch urine in men. Additional rectal/pharyngeal swabs are taken according to exposure.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A woman with chlamydial PID develops right upper quadrant pain. Perihepatitis is suspected. What is this complication called?
options: Mittelschmerz
Curling's ulcer
Budd-Chiari syndrome
Meigs syndrome
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatitis (inflammation of the liver capsule with 'violin-string' adhesions) complicating chlamydial (or gonococcal) PID, causing RUQ pain. It is a classic examinable complication of ascending genital chlamydia.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A baby born vaginally to a mother with untreated chlamydia develops a purulent conjunctivitis at 7 days of age. What is the most likely cause and an associated systemic complication?
options: Gonococcal conjunctivitis; meningitis
Chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum; pneumonia
Viral conjunctivitis; hepatitis
Chemical conjunctivitis; nil
Staphylococcal conjunctivitis; osteomyelitis
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: Vertical transmission of chlamydia causes neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum), typically presenting around 5–14 days, and can also cause chlamydial pneumonia. (Gonococcal ophthalmia tends to present earlier, in the first few days.)

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A sexually active 24-year-old woman is diagnosed with chlamydia. She reports oral and anal sex with her partner. What is the most appropriate testing approach?
options: Test the vulvovaginal site only, whatever the exposure
Send only a first-catch urine sample
Send a blood test for chlamydia antibodies
Test all sites of exposure — vulvovaginal, rectal and pharyngeal — and offer a full STI screen
Test only if she develops symptoms at those sites
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: Test all sites of exposure — vulvovaginal, rectal and pharyngeal — and offer a full STI screen
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: Chlamydia should be tested at all sites of potential exposure: vulvovaginal swab plus rectal (anal sex) and pharyngeal (oral sex) swabs. A full STI screen (gonorrhoea, syphilis, HIV) should also be offered, as coinfection is common.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: Regarding the 3-month re-test recommended after a positive chlamydia result, what is its purpose?
options: To detect reinfection, as young positive patients are at high risk of a new infection
To confirm the original treatment cured the infection
To check for antibiotic resistance
To screen the patient's partner
To confirm the NAAT has become negative
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: To detect reinfection, as young positive patients are at high risk of a new infection
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: The 3-month re-test after a positive result is designed to detect reinfection (common in this high-risk group), NOT to confirm cure — treatment is highly effective, so a test of cure is not routinely needed. Any test of cure, when indicated, is done separately at ≥3–5 weeks.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A 22-year-old man with a penicillin allergy and no other issues is diagnosed with uncomplicated urethral chlamydia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: He cannot be treated because of the penicillin allergy
Benzathine penicillin after desensitisation
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days — penicillin allergy is not relevant
Ceftriaxone intramuscularly
Nitrofurantoin for 5 days
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days — penicillin allergy is not relevant
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: Chlamydia is treated with doxycycline, which is unrelated to penicillin, so a penicillin allergy is irrelevant. First-line remains doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days. (Penicillins are not used for chlamydia at all.)

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: Which statement about the presentation of chlamydia is most accurate?
options: It is symptomatic in almost all infected people
Women are always symptomatic while men are not
It always causes a purulent urethral discharge
Symptoms reliably appear within 24 hours of exposure
It is asymptomatic in around 70% of women and 50% of men, which is the rationale for screening
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: It is asymptomatic in around 70% of women and 50% of men, which is the rationale for screening
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: Most chlamydia infections are asymptomatic (~70% of women, ~50% of men), so infection spreads silently. This asymptomatic majority is why opportunistic screening of young women aged 15-24 exists rather than relying on symptomatic presentation.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A patient with confirmed genital chlamydia is also found to have gonorrhoea on the same STI screen. Which principle does this illustrate about chlamydia management?
options: Chlamydia never coexists with other sexually transmitted infections
Coinfection is common — do a full STI screen and refer to GUM for contact tracing
Only the chlamydia needs treating when there is coinfection
Coexisting gonorrhoea makes the chlamydia untreatable
Screening for other STIs is unnecessary once chlamydia is found
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.answer: Coinfection is common — do a full STI screen and refer to GUM for contact tracing
conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.explanation: Finding chlamydia should always prompt a full STI screen because coinfection (e.g. with gonorrhoea) is common, and GUM referral for partner notification/contact tracing is standard. Both infections are then treated according to their own regimens.

conditions__SEXUAL HEALTH__Chlamydia.question: A woman treated for chlamydia with doxycycline reports she is now 5 weeks pregnant and was treated at 2 weeks' gestation before she knew. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Terminate the pregnancy due to doxycycline exposure
